It is difficult to liaise with them as the main carer about [my] parents’ needs as the care staff do not read any of my notes left or if they do they do their own thing despite [registered manager] also giving them direction and instructions.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. The provider carried out monthly informal telephone monitoring reviews of the service to check that people were happy with their care. We could see that adjustments had been made to care and support in relation to the feedback. People’s relatives were able to review care records, and we viewed comments made by relatives which had prompted changes to call times or care plans.

Complaints about the service had been received and actions had been taken to address the concerns. A person said, “My husband has contacted them regarding a query, this was dealt with very promptly to our satisfaction.” Compliments about the service were not routinely recorded, however we did listen to a voicemail note that a relative had made complimenting the staff. A local authority care manager had emailed the service after they had reviewed a person. They shared, ‘[Person] speaks very highly of the carers and is very grateful for the support, care and compassion that she has received.’ People and their relatives told us, “I have not had any concerns. If I did have a worry or concern, I trust that she would deal with it” and “I have never had a complaint or issue, but if I ring with a query, they respond quickly, and my request is dealt with to my satisfaction.” A health and social care professional said, “‘I have always found Logic Care Solutions good to work alongside, they are good at maintaining contact to keep me updated with any client needs or changes I am involved with.”

Supervisions and spot checks had taken place frequently; staff were provided with an opportunity to discuss any concerns they may have about people’s care or how it could be improved. Staff told us they had a weekly meeting to discuss important information and any concerns. A member of staff told us, “We also have group supervision, we did one last month. We do it in 2 groups and discuss cases and concerns. We get good feedback when we work together.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support. Staff could tell us how they would access additional support from healthcare professionals to help people manage their health, should they be required. The management team gave us examples of when they had made contact with people’s GP or the district nursing service when people had become unwell. A staff member said, “If medical help is needed, the manager gets help.” A person told us the service had contacted an occupational therapist who visited them.

Records showed that staff had received training to support people with their specific health or lifelong conditions, such as stoma care and dementia. Records showed staff had not undertaken training in diabetes even though they supported people who had diabetes. The provider advised they would address this, staff confirmed that diabetes training was added to their training requirements after our visit.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been ratedgood. This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was joined-up, flexible and supported choice and continuity. The service worked with other health professionals involved in people’s care. Information was shared with staff regarding any changes to people’s health or care needs. Staff told us how they supported people and their relatives. Records showed most people had consistent staff supporting them. Some people had more staff involved in their care which they did not always like. A person said, “I do like to have carers who like to know my needs and wants.”

A health and social care professional told us,

“If I have requested information from LCS (Logic Care Solutions), I have never had any issues with a response. If they feel we require updating on clients i.e. change in need, then from my experience, they act on this as appropriate. For example, they were recently allocated to one of our clients who has dementia, they kept me informed of any issues that occurred, how they overcame them and how best to approach moving forward in future and if they felt calls needed to be extended to provide the best possible support. They liaised with the family very well and reassured the family during difficult times.”

A staff member said, “We report if [people are] losing weight, dehydrated, or appearing pale or tired.” Another staff member said, “We are reassessing people whose needs have changed, we involve the OT (occupational therapist) and involve other professionals.”

Most relatives told us they felt staff communicated well them well. A relative said, “They make adjustments like when I mentioned my mum requires them to talk slower and be a little loud.” Another relative said, “I wish they would use my communication book as requested to highlight shopping I need to get.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it. People lived independently in their own homes in the community and mostly managed their own daily activities and community engagement. We had difficulty getting in contact with the service and the management team before the assessment and during the assessment because the phone lines were poor and either the caller or recipient could not hear the other person. When we were at the Logic Care Solutions office, we observed that this happened with people, staff and relatives when they called. Despite this, people and their relatives told us they were always able to make contact with the service when they needed to. People and their relatives could use the online system to review care notes and leave messages for the registered manager. The management team told us that sometimes staff supported people with additional tasks to meet their needs such as essential food shopping or liaising with the pharmacy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff and leaders did not always actively listen to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes. This meant their care was not always tailored in response to this. It was clear from some care records people had time to chat with staff as part of care visits, showing that the visits were not task focused. However, some people experienced shortened care visits, which evidenced that not everyone had the same experience. The registered manager carried out spot checks to ensure people had equal opportunities and positive experiences from the care provided. After the assessment the registered manager told us, “For shortened calls, this seems to be happening a lot but with some clients. Carers do not leave till the tasks are completed and would usually check with the clients if it was okay to leave. Often, the clients are happy for them to leave once they have completed the tasks. They will stay longer at other times if the need arises or there is an unexpected delay. However, this is an issue I am targeting with the carers, and we have decided to check and take disciplinary action if the situation persists. I assure you they are not rushing or shortening calls to get to the next client or finish early.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result. People were offered opportunities to feedback about the service; the registered manager showed us surveys which some people had completed, 9 surveys had been completed in 2025, all of which contained positive feedback. The provider sent these to people every 3 months. The provider carried out monthly telephone monitoring calls. People and relatives told us that the service was responsive to their needs. A person told us, “[Registered manager] did visit week the before last and we discussed a change in carers. The manager is good she knows what I want and what I don’t want.” Staff described how they listened to and respected people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not always work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. Some care plans were very detailed in relation to most areas of people’s care and support needs. Some care plans lacked detail, these were amended by the management team during the assessment. It was not evident that people or their relatives had been involved in the reviews, changes and amendments to the care plans. Oral care was lacking in the care plans and within the care records. A person who required full support with all of their personal care needs had a task ‘oral care’ written in their care plan twice a day. However, the care plan itself did not give staff instructions around this, or detail if the person had dentures or their own teeth. We reviewed their care records and found no entries to show staff had supported with this. It was not clear that people were having their needs met in relation to their oral health care. Staff had not been recording when they had offered teeth cleaning support or when people had declined.

Relatives told us the care and support met their loved ones needs. A relative said, “I was unhappy [with the previous agency] which is why I switched to this agency. This agency checked with me if I was happy with them and the changes made which I was. I have been involved in my mother’s care and decisions from the beginning.” People told us they enjoyed the company of the staff that knew them well. A person said, “I have the same staff all day.” Staff told us they enjoyed the company of the people they supported.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary: People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life. Some people had a DNACPR (Do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation) form in place. This is an advanced decision not to attempt CPR. It is not about other treatments or care. Some staff told us they had received training to support them to provide end of life care when needed. Staff knowledge of end-of-life support was varied. At the time of the assessment, no one was at the end of their life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. People were able to access information. The provider had an accessible information policy in place. The service supported people with a variety of communication needs. No one had written information provided to them in different forms at the time of the assessment. The registered manager told us information could be made available in a variety of ways to meet people’s needs. They explained a person had their letters read to them. Staff were aware of people’s individual communication needs for example, people who may have hearing or vision impairments. A person did not speak English as a first language, when there was difficulty in understanding the person’s relative acted as translator.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated requires improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment, the management of people’s medicines and deployment and training of staff.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly. The provider had an up-to-date infection prevention and control (IPC) policy. Staff had completed IPC training. Staff told us they had access to personal protective equipment (PPE) to keep themselves and people safe. A staff member said, “I have PPE in my car, and we can go to the office to pick up more, such as shoe covers, aprons and sanitiser.” The provider carried out spot checks of staff practice which included checks to make sure staff were using PPE appropriately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. Risks to people were not always identified and risk assessments lacked enough detailed information for staff to know how to keep people safe. For example, we found some evidence in people’s daily notes which showed risk assessments were not being followed. Comments included, “People’s needs change especially when they have gone to hospital and come back. If they are new, we are given guidelines on what to do, we report things and changes” and “Care plans are outdated and do not reflect their current needs.” There were no risk assessments in place for staff transporting people into the community in their own vehicles. People who were at risk of choking had risk assessments in place which listed staff were to cut food into small pieces, but the risk assessment did not provide information about what size those pieces should be and did not refer to people’s speech and language therapy assessments or IDDSI (The International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative) guidance. This put people at risk of harm.

There were anticoagulant risk assessments in place for some people who were prescribed this medicine. Not everyone prescribed anticoagulants had a risk assessment in place to detail safe ways of working for staff. The anticoagulant risk assessments that were in place did not highlight risks to people if they fell and what action staff should take. Diabetes risk assessments were not in place. We reported our concerns to the registered manager during the assessment process, and they arranged for amendments to be made to make risk assessments clearer for staff.

We received mixed feedback from staff in relation to the management of risks. Some staff we spoke with did not know the signs and symptoms of low or high blood sugars for people diagnosed with diabetes.

Despite the evidence above, people and relatives told us they and their loved ones were safe and staff knew them well.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. They did not listen to concerns about safety and did not investigate or report safety events. Lessons were not learnt to continually identify and embed good practice. We could not be assured people benefitted from a service that learned lessons from incident and accidents and put measures in place to reduce the likelihood of these reoccurring. Accidents and incidents had not always been reviewed and dealt with by the management team in a timely manner. Staff told us they completed accidents and incident forms when people had fallen. The registered manager told us a number of times there had been no accidents and falls. When we challenged this based on examples given by staff the registered manager told us there had been falls. They then explained they had taken action to create a falls monitoring form to record falls for use when staff witnessed falls, but expected a different procedure for unwitnessed falls. They explained they would consider how to mitigate reoccurrence. The registered manager acknowledged that not all incidents raised by staff had been logged, and explained this was an issue they were looking into. The registered manager told us they were going to ensure incident forms were logged and actions and lessons learnt would be incorporated into the process.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. People were not involved in planning. Medicines were not well managed. People were not always having their medicines as prescribed which had the potential to cause them harm. Medicines administration records (MAR) showed gaps in recording and daily records did not evidence medicines had been administered as prescribed. A person had not had their Vitamin D medicine for more than 1 month. Staff had been recording the medicine as not given or out of stock. The call monitoring system had not flagged up to the management team that the person had not received medicines as prescribed. We reported this to the registered manager who took action with the person’s relative to amend arrangements for who would order and collect medicines. A person’s MAR showed that staff had been signing the medicines to show they had given them. However, staff had not administered the medicines as they had left them in a pot for the person to take when they awoke. This meant the provider could not be assured the person had received medicines as prescribed. The person told us that staff arrived too early in the day to provide care and support. They told us, “They give me medication but if I’m asleep they leave them by my bed.”

Staff told us they received training and competency checks in relation to medicines. Comments included, “I give prescription medicines and am competency checked and trained. I don’t give anything outside the prescription, some medicine is needed PRN (as and when required medicines)” and “I have done medicines training and have done medicines competency, we do it regularly.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They did not work together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. They made sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. Whilst the staffing rota showed staff had time between care calls, staff reported that the time was not always adequate. Staff were starting their care calls earlier than scheduled to get ahead. Staff told us they had not always been given adequate time on their rota to travel between care calls which meant they were late for care visits, or they started very early in the morning to get ahead. Comments included, “Travel time is a dicey thing. We don’t get enough travel time; it’s not totally a management fault. Most service users want the time, and we work around it. There are lots of roadworks currently. We call and say we are running late. Sometimes we leave early in the morning to start calls early. We do not cut calls short”; “We have enough time to travel, if we have an issue such as a blocked road, we call the manager. We don’t keep clients waiting and don’t cut short times” and “We have travel time, and we start early to get a head start and to be able to get through all the calls. Travel time isn’t all that much.”

We found evidence in people’s daily records that they were having shortened calls. Some electronic call monitoring records showed some people were having very short care visits. Several people had a 30-minute care call scheduled and records showed a person had a 3 minute visit on 21 February 2025. Another person was getting approximately 10 minutes of their 30 minutes provided each day in May 2025. Some people were having their care visits very early and not at a time that suited them. This meant staff were leaving medicines out for them and doing tasks whilst the person was sleeping. The person’s daily records confirmed this.

People and relatives gave us mixed views about their experience of staff providing care and support at the right time for them. Comments included, “If they come at 06.30, I am asleep, so they leave me in bed, and I have to sort my own pads out. If I wake up at 08.30 to 09.00, they give me a strip wash, but I have to ask them to. They give me breakfast. Most days they leave me in bed. I have rung the manager when they came one and a half hours late”; “She (staff member) arrives on time and stays the full duration”; “The staff don’t always stay for the duration of their visit. If they complete all the tasks they are meant to, and I am happy then I don’t make a fuss of it" and “They have always come around the time they are supposed to be here and have not missed one out.”

Staff did not always have the right training to meet people’s needs. No staff had attended diabetes training despite supporting people with diabetes. Staff were allocated this training during the inspection after we raised it with the registered manager. Staff did not have a good understanding of diabetes despite having just completed the training. Only 2 out of 21 staff had completed dysphagia training despite staff supporting people who had difficulty swallowing and receiving food and fluids which were tailored to their assessed needs. Spot checks and supervisions were taking place. Staff told us they received induction, support, supervision and training. A staff member said, ‘[Registered manager] does spot checks, she did one on Sunday unannounced. Supervision is every 3 to 4 months. I have had 2 this year already.”

Before and after we inspected the service, we received information of concern about sponsorship licences for staff. We reported these to the UK Visa and Immigration service. We examined 3 staff files, and all of the required checks had been carried out and documents were all in date. In files we saw copies of references, interview notes, photographic identification and Disclosure and Barring Service forms (DBS). DBS checks provide information including details about convictions and cautions held on the Police National Computer. The information helps employers make safer recruitment decisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not always make sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.Risks relating to the environments staff were working in had not been fully assessed. For example, risks relating to access, egress, flooring, lighting, location of emergency shut offs for gas, electric and water. We discussed this with the registered manager. They advised they would review the risk assessments and add additional information to ensure staff had all the information they needed to keep themselves and people safe. During the assessment process some of these were put in place, however they contained conflicting information.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always work well with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not always manage or monitor people’s safety. They did not always make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services. The provider carried out assessments of people’s needs prior to their package of care and support starting. This enabled them to meet people in their own homes. Staff told us care plans and risk assessments were in place when they carried out their care and support visits. However, the structure of these assessments varied and not all relevant information had been recorded within the assessment to create detailed care plans for staff to follow. For example, important information about allergies, religion and assessments of the environments were missing. This meant staff did not have all the information they needed to understand people’s care and support needs, wishes and preferences. We received mixed feedback from staff about care plans and assessments. Comments included, “A female client needs reassessing, and this has been raised over the last year”; “No care plans are updated, [person] has a care plan that states she must have someone sit whilst she eats but she is independent” and “I always check care plans and risk assessments for new clients and it gives me information on what to expect.” People and relatives told us their needs were assessed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately. People were safe and were protected from harm. Safeguarding and whistleblowing policies were in place and were accessible to staff. Staff were aware of the safeguarding policy. A member of staff said, “Safeguarding adults at risk this was face to face (training) and I have also done the theory. I have not had to do one but have raised concerns with my manager who has taken this forward.” Another staff member said, “I have done safeguarding. I reported to the manager as I had a client who was being financially abused by a relative. I reported it and it was sorted. I can speak to CQC if I was not listened to.” People and their relatives told us they felt safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated requires improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to governance at the service and notifying CQC of important events.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Not all leaders understood the context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. They did not always embody the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not always have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively, or they did not always do so with integrity, openness and honesty.

Some staff felt they were not listened to by the management team when they raised issues and concerns. Staff said, “[Registered manager] is very responsive and approachable. I feel listened to”; “We are supported, they listen and they motivate”; “There is no support, and we are always told we can’t be losing money even at the detriment of staff” and “They listen to you when you are there then when you leave, they will ring the person and tell them what you have said and you become the black sheep. I have been told keep quiet by other carers.”

Services providing health and social care to people are required to inform the CQC of important events that happen in the service. This is so we can check that appropriate action has been taken. Concerns were not always reported to CQC when they should have been. The provider had not informed CQC of notifiable incidents such as safeguarding alerts. The concerns were reported to the local authority as an accusation of abuse, but a notification was not sent to CQC, and it needed to be as this is a legal requirement. After the assessment visit the registered manager submitted these in retrospect. Other notifications had been submitted as appropriate.

The management team knew people well and were passionate about making sure people received good quality care. Staff understood their responsibilities to meet regulatory requirements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: People did not feel they could speak up and that their voice would be heard. Staff confirmed they were invited to meetings and encouraged to contribute. However, they did not always feel listened to. A staff member said, “Issue with raising things as the management are all family, I think there is only 1 person in the office who is not related.” Some staff told us they were encouraged to voice their ideas for improvements and any concerns. The provider had a whistle blowing policy in place. However, we received mixed feedback from staff about how to raise concerns with the provider or outside organisations if they needed to. Some staff said they don’t feel listened to and would not raise concerns. Another member of staff said, “I would whistle blow if it is not right.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate. The provider had systems in place to check the quality of the service. Some audits had been carried out. There were monthly audits of infection control, hand hygiene, medicines, and staff files. The audits were not always robust enough to highlight and manage shortfalls and areas for improvement in the service. For example, the audit of training had not identified that staff had not completed diabetes training and the issues with medicines. Audits had not detected that care plans and risk assessments were lacking detail and were not always up to date and accurate. There were no audits of accidents and incidents. Where audits had found actions that needed addressing, actions had been recorded, and the management team had signed off items that had been addressed.

The provider had not been following their own complaints policy. Complaints had not been formally acknowledged and when the complaint had been investigated, the complainant did not receive a formal outcome. A person told us, “When I complain, the manager does nothing. I’ve given up on them.”

People's personal records were stored securely including on computers and applications on devices, these were protected by passwords, so that only staff who had been authorised to access the information could do so.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not always encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They did not always actively contribute to safe, effective practice and research. The local authority quality monitoring team had been supporting the service for some time with trying to improve the quality of care plans and risk assessments. They told us the provider had been using an electronic care plan system which had brought about some improvements. They advised, “There is still work to be done. Provider continues to send documents to assess but improvement is slow.” During the assessment we found that the provider and registered manager had not embedded the advice and guidance from the local authority across the service to ensure care plans and risk assessments were consistent, detailed and robust.

The registered manager told us they had reviewed the feedback we gave them as part of the onsite and offsite assessment process and valued this. They were using the feedback to make improvements to the service and to put systems in place to embed the changes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement. The registered manager was keen to build links with partnership agencies and had liaised with the local authority and local integrated care board. The registered manager was involved in forums and events to keep abreast of local and national developments in health and social care. The registered manager gained peer support from other registered managers and providers within the care system.

A local authority care manager told us that the service had been responsive when complaints or concerns had come up. They fed back that a person had told them that some staff had been talking in their own language when providing care and support which made the person feel uncomfortable. They told us,

“This issue was raised to [registered manager]. I contacted the client the following day, client was very happy. [Registered manager] had been to visit and apologised for any issues that she has come across and noted that it was not acceptable for the carers to do this and that she would speak with the carers directly and ensure that this does not happen again. Client was very pleased, she reported that [registered manager] is very understanding, and a wonderful person and that [registered manager] will contact her in one month to see how she is and if there are any other issues.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have a clear shared vision, strategy and culture which was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not always understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities.The staff gave mixed feedback about the culture of the service. Some staff reported a positive open culture where they felt empowered to raise any concerns or make suggestions. Other staff gave negative feedback. Comments included, “It is good”; “The culture is not perfect, she encourages us to sort it out amongst ourselves”; “There is no confidentiality the manager will tell the other person what you said, and this can cause problems” and “Cannot share anything about other carers or personal stuff. Very good around client’s confidentiality.” The registered manager and staff were passionate about the service and wanted to ensure people had good quality care and improved outcomes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. The registered manager told us staff care packages included; flexible working, during fasting staff were offered support, time off to go to church, support during Eid, Christmas and other celebrations. Staff had access to the Blue Light card (discount service for social care sector). The registered manager pointed staff towards money off and offers, ran a recommend a friend scheme, offered employee support to gain mental health support and access to counsellors.

Staff told us they were supported where necessary with reasonable adjustments in relation to their personal, health or religious needs such as changes to shift patterns to support childcare arrangements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
