asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Rapid Care - Archived
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of Assessment: 01 April to 26 April 2025. The service is a care at home service providing support to people living in their own homes. At the time of our assessment the service was supporting 99 people with the regulated activity ‘Personal Care’.

This assessment was undertaken in response to concerns in relation to risk management and safe and effective staffing of the service.

We identified 2 continued breaches of the legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment and good governance.

Risks to people continued to not always be fully assessed and detailed guidance was not always in place to mitigate risks. People’s medicines were not always managed safely. There were enough staff to meet people’s needs. However, people told us staff did not always stay for the duration of their agreed call times and records confirmed this. The provider was aware and had begun to take action to address this.

The service worked with other professionals to meet people’s needs. However, systems and processes had not always been used effectively by staff and management to ensure concerns with or barriers to people’s care were addressed in a timely manner. The governance systems had not always been robust and continued to not be effective at identifying areas for improvement.

However, people received person-centred care with their choices and rights respected. Staff were kind and compassionate and supported people to maintain their independence.

In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/ or appeals have been concluded.We have also asked the provider for an action plan in response to some of the concerns found at this assessment.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: People and relatives were overall happy with the service they received and told us they would recommend the service. Comments from people and relatives included, “We consider them to be a safe a caring service.”, “Very happy with the service.” And, “We cannot fault the service we receive as the carers are very friendly and perform their tasks efficiently and thoughtfully.” However, some people and relatives gave mixed feedback about the staffing of the service and felt this could be better managed.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider and staff team promoted people’s independence and supported them to have choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing. A relative told us, “The staff listen to [loved one], there is a particular top [loved one] likes to wear, so they always dress [loved one] in that top.” Staff gave examples of how they supported people to make choices and maintain their independence. A staff member said, “Give people choices, things like clothing, where they want to go, if they want to wash or shower and what they want to use during that. Perfume or anything like that. It’s about asking and building that bond with the person."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider always treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Feedback from people and relatives about the care provided by staff was positive. Comments included, “Staff are caring, kind and compassionate.”, “carers are very friendly to [loved one] …[their] face lights up when [staff] come in and they have a bit of banter.” And “Staff are gentle and careful when using the hoist to help [loved one] move.” Staff supported people with kindness and compassion. They knew people well, their needs and how they liked their care delivered. The provider had oversight of the quality of care being delivered by staff through regular spot checks of the care provided.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The systems and processes within the service were not always being operated effectively to ensure that the provider had oversight of what people’s immediate needs were and whether these were being met. For example, staff raising changes or concerns with people’s care. This meant administrative actions required to ensure people’s immediate needs were being met had not always been completed in a timely manner as evidenced under the safe domain for example in relation to missed medicines.

However, staff responded to people’s immediate needs during their care calls. Feedback from people and relatives was positive about the care provided by staff. A person shared, “The carers are good at what they do, they are attentive, helpful and always try to engage in conversation.” A relative said, “Carers are patient and attentive, helping [loved one] to feel comfortable during personal care.” People and relatives fedback that the service was flexible when needs changed to put in additional care calls. A staff member shared an example of when they had supported a person following a fall to successfully re-build their confidence and begin to mobilise again.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. Some relatives gave examples of how staff respected their loved one’s personal preferences and interests. A relative said, “The staff understand [loved one’s] preferences, including [their] preferred shower time.” Another relative said, “Staff know [loved one] likes books, so they always bring different books for [them]. Staff were knowledgeable about the people they supported and were mindful of their individual strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff. Staff told us their well-being was supported, and they were enabled to complete their roles through adequate training and supervision. Staff felt listened to when they raised concerns. One staff member gave an example of changes that had been made to their rota to support their personal needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure people's needs were assessed before they began delivering people's packages of care. The registered manager told us care coordinators spoke with people and their relatives to assess their support needs and preferences. People and relatives told us they had been involved in their assessments. A relative told us they were, “Satisfied with the care Rapid provides, the staff are helpful, understanding, and attentive to loved one’s dementia and mobility needs.” Another relative gave an example of how their loved ones needs had recently changed and staff adapted the care provided to meet their loved ones needs. Staff told us they reported any changes in people's needs to the managers or the office. However, we found this was not always done consistently and the management systems and processes in place had not always been effectively operated to ensure changes were robustly identified and updated.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment. Most people felt staff sought their consent each time they entered their homes and supported them with their personal care. Staff told us they respected people's wishes in relation to their care and treatment and understood the principles of the Mental Capacity Act. Staff described how they supported people to make choices they were able to. A staff member said, “Ask client with dementia what they want rather than just making it for them. If someone suffering badly only give 2 choices, if more capacity give a range of options.” Where people lacked capacity appropriate others were involved in decisions about their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards. For example, a relative told us, “[Loved one had] a bedsore. While the district nurse handled the dressings, I believe the healing was largely due to the carers’ efforts in carefully positioning [loved one] and providing consistent, thoughtful care.”

Processes were in place to support people with their nutrition and hydration needs. People’s care records contained information in relation to the safety of their swallow, their appetite, level of independence and preferences. Staff were aware of these needs and delivered people’s support in line with their planned care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. A relative told us staff worked well with another agency that was involved in supporting their loved one’s needs. Staff worked in partnership with each other as well as healthcare professionals to ensure people's needs were met. A staff member gave an example of how they had sought a second opinion regarding a pressure damaged area for a person they support to ensure the person received the care they required. Staff told us they checked the care records for previous care notes to ensure they were up to date on people’s needs and identified any changes or issues with the person's care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had not always monitored and improved outcomes for people. For example, we identified examples of where staff had identified potential issues with people's care and instances where staff had not delivered or recorded people’s care as planned. These had not always been escalated in a timely manner to ensure people experienced positive outcomes. For example, concerns in relation to a person’s well-being.

However, some other people felt they had been supported to achieve good outcomes. A person told us, “[The service] enabled [them] to remain in [their] own home rather than moving into residential care.”

Staff felt they had supported people to achieve good outcomes and gave examples of how they had encouraged people to mobilise and this had enabled people to become more independent with their mobility.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. A person said, “[The service was] very caring and supportive when I have been ill.” The management team and staff were proactive in seeking support and advice from other professionals to support people’s health and welfare needs.

Staff supported people to live healthier lives for example, supporting them to eat and drink or taking people to any appointments where required for their health and welfare. A staff member told us, “When some of the clients have appointments to see GP or Doctor some don’t like it so you need to speak to the client and encourage them to be strong and healthy. Some client’s staff do go with [to appointments]."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Some people and relatives felt that they had not always received continuity of care. They fedback that they frequently had their care provided by different carers and they would like consistency.

Records did not always contain up to date information about people’s needs or detailed guidance about how to provide people’s required care. This meant there was a risk staff may not provide consistent care for people and staff had to rely on each other to know how to support some people safely and in line with their preferences.

Staff told us they felt confident they provided continuity in care as they worked with other staff who knew people well and learnt how to carry out the care calls. Staff also said the care tasks required were listed on their service’s system. Staff marked them as complete during calls which they felt supported them to consistently meet people’s needs.

Some people and relatives were positive about the service provision. A relative said, “The team is responsive, consistent and fully understanding of [loved one’s] needs."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it. The provider had not always ensured people’s needs were supported in full in a timely manner for example, some people had not received their prescribed medicines which the provider had not identified or addressed until we raised it with them during our inspection.

Staff supported people during care calls to have equal access to things they needed. For example, staff left drinks, snacks and walking aids within reach of people at the end of their care calls to ensure they were able to support themselves safely in between their care calls.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this. The management team told us they sent quality monitoring surveys to people and gave examples of action they had taken to improve the service based on the feedback received although feedback was positive from those who responded. The management team were aware some people preferred telephone contact while others preferred written contact, and staff were available to support people where necessary to share their views. The provider also carried out spot checks to ensure people had equal opportunities and experience from the care provided.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. People and relatives told us they felt listened to, they shared examples of when they had raised concerns or suggestions and how these had been acted on. Staff supported people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. A staff member shared an example which demonstrated how they supported a person to raise a concern about the arrangement for their care call and how this resulted in a positive change to their arrangement which improved the person’s experience of their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had not always made sure that the systems and processes in place supported staff to deliver person-centred care. Some care records did not contain detailed person-centred guidance about how to meet people’s individual needs. This meant all staff including newer staff did not have access to guidance which would enable them to provide a consistent level of person-centred care.

However, staff were passionate about providing person-centred care. A staff member said, “[People are] at the centre of their care; wants, needs and desires met and advocating for them. Engage clients and wear what they want to, eat what they want to and wellbeing is met, receiving the best care for their well-being.” People and relatives felt staff met their individual needs and records of the daily care people received supported this. A relative gave an example of how their loved one experienced discomfort from an injury and found massage helpful, the relative told us staff made this a priority.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life. Staff were aware of people’s decision about their care should they become unwell or in a medical emergency and people’s decisions were clearly recorded in their care records.

The provider had also assessed and planned to ensure contingencies were in place to minimise any disruption to people’s care in the event of company wide emergencies.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. People and relatives had access to information and feedback from most was that communication was good. Some relatives fedback that information was not always accurate or accessible in the service’s care app. For example, a relative told us they could not always access copies of the staff rota to see who would be delivering their loved ones care in advance. Staff were aware of people’s individual communication needs which were recorded in their care records. For example, staff were aware of people who may have vision impairments and ensured people had access to their glasses.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement. This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service continued to be in breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment and the ways people’s medicines were managed safely.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. Infection prevention and control training formed part of the mandatory staff training. The provider carried out spot checks on staff to ensure staff were following correct practice. Staff were aware of how to prevent the risk of infection. One staff member told us, “Always use the [Personal Protective Equipment], wash hands well and dry well and use sanitiser.” Most people told us staff followed good infection control procedures although some commented not all staff did this. A person said, “the staff maintain cleanliness, wash their hands, wear gloves and aprons.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. At our last assessment we found concerns with the level of detail in people’s risk assessments and care plans. At this assessment we found not enough improvement had been made. Some care records such as risk assessments and care plans still did not contain enough detail for staff to follow for each person. Records in relation to catheter care and moving and handling still did not consistently have detailed information about how to identify concerns such as infection or how to use people’s mobility equipment safely for the person.

Although staff were knowledgeable about the signs of infection there was not detailed guidance and there was a risk newer staff may not identify these concerns. There was not clear recording of when to escalate concerns and there was not always evidence that concerns were escalated to the provider in a timely manner. For one person we saw they were experiencing issues with their catheter for an extended period of time, although staff had highlighted this in the person’s daily records of care, the provider could not demonstrate these concerns had been regularly followed up by the management at Rapid Care to ensure the concern was dealt with swiftly.

However, people and relatives felt involved in the development of risk assessments and care plans and felt safe with the care provided.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had a positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. There was a system in place to report accidents and incidents. Staff reported accidents or incidents for action by the management team. Staff told us they felt confident to raise concerns and gave examples of how learning was implemented following incidents such as, “re-doing training, chat with manager or shadowing to refresh our skills.” However, we found some incidents had not been fully actioned in a timely manner. The management team did not always meet with staff in a timely manner to discuss concerns. This meant staff were not consistently supported to learn and development to improve people’s experience of their care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Medicines were not always managed safely. We received mixed feedback about the support people received with their medicines. A relative told us they frequently had to remind staff to use correct prescribed creams for their loved one.

We found some people had not received some medicines for extended periods of time. There were no actions recorded within people’s records to highlight this to management to be addressed so people would receive their correct medicine.

The provider had not followed their own policy in relation to the recording of people’s medicines. For example, there were no medicine administration records for those who were prompted with their medicines as stated in their policy. Some people’s records did not include medicines staff were administering. This meant that staff may not always know when people have had their medicines and what medicines they need. There was a risk people might not receive the right treatment. There was no guidance in place for prescribed creams and pain relief patches to guide staff on where to apply these. This meant people were at risk of not receiving their medicines as prescribed. The registered manager began to put guidance in place for the people we identified during our assessment.

There was not a robust, effectively operated system in place to provide complete oversight of medicines to ensure these were being managed safely for people.

Staff told us they had received medicine training and had their competency assessed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. However, feedback from people and relatives was mixed about the staffing at Rapid Care. Although most relatives and people felt staff arrived on time; some fed back that staff were frequently arriving late, with a person stating there was no prior communication about this. A relative said this impacted on their loved one’s daily routine.

Many people and relatives told us that staff did not stay for the full duration of their care calls, however, none told us this negatively impacted on their needs being met. Call monitoring records showed that staff were not always staying for the full duration of people’s care calls and it was not always recorded in daily logs that people had agreed to this.

The registered manager told us there were systems and processes in place to monitor whether staff arrived at their calls and stayed for long enough. They told us they audited data about people’s care calls and had recently addressed short call lengths with staff. The manager was monitoring some staffs performance in relation to this and had asked all staff to record more clearly when they were excused early from people’s care calls.

Staff were now recruited safely, with an induction process and training in place. Staff felt their training was sufficient to support them to carry out their roles.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider completed environmental risk assessments which detected and controlled potential risks to staff and people’s care within their own homes. For example, staff identified a fire risk and encouraged the family to address this. The provider made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care. A person told us they felt safe when staff supported them with their mobility. Staff felt confident they maintained safe care environments. A staff member told us, “When we go in [to people’s homes] we make sure walkways are clear and areas are clean."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. The provider carried out initial assessments of people’s needs before their support started. Referrals were made to relevant healthcare professionals to ensure people received the care and support they required. A person told us, “The service has provided exemplary care since [their] discharge home.” Staff told us they shadowed calls before they started providing a person’s care to keep consistency for people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. A person told us they, “feel safe in [staff’s] care.” Relatives felt their loved ones were safe when receiving care from staff at Rapid Care.

Staff understood how to report safeguarding concerns and felt confident these would be acted on. A staff member said, “Safeguarding to me means protecting people’s wellbeing, information and things like that, that makes sure they are getting the best quality of care. Making sure they are not harmed in calls and reporting back if I suspect abuse or neglect.”

There were systems in place to escalate safeguarding concerns and the provider had notified the local authority and the commission appropriately. A safeguarding audit was completed by registered manager to ensure systems and processes were being followed to support the service to safeguard people. Where actions had been identified these had been completed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement. This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service continued to be in breach of legal regulation in relation to governance at the service.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Staff felt the service was managed by capable and compassionate leaders. A staff member said, the provider and registered manager carried out their roles well. They said, “[The provider] is very professional, very hard working, [the provider] is always approachable if you have a problem. [The registered manager] is a good manager always on the phone 24 hours a day."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard. There was a whistleblowing policy in place which outlined the process for raising concerns. Staff knew how to raise concerns inside and outside the organisation. Staff told us they felt comfortable with their individual line managers and the registered manager and felt able to tell them any concerns.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to not always have clear systems of accountability or good governance. Governance systems to assess, monitor and mitigate risk had not been operated effectively. Robust processes were not in place to effectively review service users’ care records. For example, the issues we found in relation to detailed and up to date guidance in people’s care records had not consistently been identified. Records in relation to people’s care were not always accurate or complete. We found instances where the care recorded for people conflicted which meant the provider could not have effective oversight of the care people received to ensure it was safe and effective.

Robust governance processes were not in place to support the safe management of medicines, and the provider had failed to ensure staff were following the services policy in relation to medicine management.

The registered manager told us they were behind on auditing records of people’s daily care and the actions required on the system. This meant some issues with people’s care had not been identified and managed in a timely manner.

Some people and relatives felt the service was not very well managed in terms of their care call monitoring and scheduling.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. After our last inspection the provider told us they would take action to address breaches of regulation in relation to safe care and treatment. They said they would make people’s risk assessments and care plans more focused to address risk. However, at this inspection risk assessments and care plans still did not consistently contain detailed and sufficient person-centered guidance for staff to follow to ensure service users’ individual risks and needs were met and managed safely. To address the previous breach of good governance the provider told us all managers would be assisting in operating and monitoring audit systems. However, at this inspection, audits had still not been operated effectively. The registered manager’s care file audit and previous medicine audit records did not contain details of what had been audited, any findings from the audit or actions taken. The date these tasks were completed was all that was recorded in the record. This meant the provider could not effectively evaluate and improve the practice at the service.

The provider had not always used the quality assurance processes to continuously learn and improve effectively for example to consider patterns or trends overtime from audits or feedback received which could help the service develop and improve.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. People, relatives and staff were positive about the partnership working in the service with other agencies, and healthcare professionals.

Staff spoke positively about learning from other professionals. A staff member said, “We usually work with [Occupational Therapists (OT)] once in a while they come to assess clients when they come we usually work with them. Aside from our training, they give details and OT teaches you. It is put in the care plan."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. Staff were positive about the culture of the service and described good team working. A staff member said, “I would say I am proud of the company, when I speak to clients, they are happy with the care they receive. I know the company has a good reputation and feel proud to be part of company that has that reputation. Clients recommend us to other people which I think speaks volumes for the company.” People and relatives confirmed they would recommend the care provided by Rapid Care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture. Staff had a good understanding of equality, diversity and inclusion and what to do if they did not feel this was supported, this was underpinned by training they had completed about equality, diversity and human rights. A staff member said, “You would never treat anyone differently based on skin colour, beliefs, anything like that. If you feel you’re discriminated against let manager know."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Rapid Care
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of Assessment: 13 and 19 January 2026. The service is a care at home service providing support to people living in their own homes. At the time of our assessment, the service was supporting 82 people with the regulated activity ‘Personal Care’.

This was a focused assessment undertaken to follow up on the enforcement action we had taken.

We identified 2 continued breaches of the legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment and good governance.

Although there had been an improvement in the assessment and management of risks identified at the last assessment, such as catheter care, we found 6 out of 7 people’s care records reviewed either did not fully assess or clearly plan for how to mitigate some people’s risks. There were multiple areas where key risk assessments or detailed guidance in people’s care plans were missing or incomplete, including for safe use of bedrails, choking risks, skin integrity risks and risks associated with people’s health conditions. The provider had made some improvement in how some medicines were managed such as clearer administration protocols for prescribed creams, but further improvements were needed.

The provider had not always taken sufficient timely action to drive improvement in all areas of the service. Governance arrangements remained inconsistent and had not been fully effective in identifying or addressing ongoing risks.

The provider had worked with external consultants and introduced new audits; some actions had led to improvements, while other areas needed further work to ensure robust and effective oversight. During the assessment, we found that new medicines audits failed to identify some of the issues we found at this assessment such as 2 people who did not have medicine administration records for their medicines.

Leaders were receptive to feedback and demonstrated a willingness to learn and improve. Action was taken promptly during the assessment to begin to address the issues found. The nominated individual also changed during the assessment, and they implemented further changes to strengthen governance and oversight at the service. These improvements were still new and not yet embedded.

However, feedback from people and relatives about the service continued to be positive. People told us they felt safe, and staff knew how to safeguard people. There were systems and processes in place to support staff to work in partnership with other relevant professionals to meet people’s needs. Staff knew people well and spoke confidently about their roles and responsibilities.

 

We have asked the provider for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People and relatives consistently told us they felt safe with staff. People and relatives said they were involved in developing care plans and that staff responded when people’s needs changed, including contacting GPs or district nurses when required. Relatives of people with more complex health needs felt staff had the skills to support them safely, particularly in relation to catheter care. People’s end‑of‑life care was described as compassionate and supportive, contributing to a sense of coordinated, holistic care.

People and relatives were confident in the support staff delivered and described staff as, “Kind”, “Caring” and “Respectful”. People felt staff knew them well and delivered person-centred care in ways that upheld dignity and promoted comfort. Comments included “The carers are all so kind, caring and very understanding.” and “This is the best service I have used; it’s all about me, which it should be.”

Some people identified minor areas where they felt the service could be strengthened. For example, some people and relatives told us that communication with office staff and the manager could be inconsistent, and some said they did not always know which carers would be visiting. Other people were positive. A person commented, “I have the same carers and they are regular, all of them being very good.”

Most people told us staff arrived within the expected time window and informed them if delays occurred. However, several people said they would like more consistent communication about which carers were attending and when, and some said they were not always informed when carers were running late.

Overall, people and relatives were positive about the care and support provided. A person said, “What can I say, I couldn’t ask for anymore. From the manager, office staff and all my carers it makes my care complete. I receive an excellent service."

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment, we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment, the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe, and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in continued breach of legal regulation in relation to people’s safe care and treatment, including the ways people’s medicines were managed.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection.

Staff followed appropriate infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. People told us staff used personal protective equipment correctly and maintained hygiene standards. A person said, “[Staff were] very respectful and always clean and tidy.” Staff had completed IPC training, and daily notes demonstrated safe cleaning and personal care practices. The provider staff IPC compliance as part of their quality monitoring during spot checks on staff practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.

People told us they were involved in their care planning, and relatives agreed. A relative told us, “[Staff] discuss things with us and keep us updated.” The provider had focused on addressing previous concerns with some areas of risk assessment, monitoring and mitigation. Improvements were seen in some care records and task instructions, for example, around catheter care and moving and handling support.

However, some other risk assessments were missing or incomplete, such as for bedrails and skin integrity risks. This meant there was a risk that staff would not be aware of risks to people and people could be at risk of avoidable harm. We raised this concern with the provider during the assessment and immediate actions were taken to address gaps.

Some people were at increased risk of infection related to their personal care and support needs. Although the risk of infection had been considered for catheter care, this had not always been considered for skin integrity concerns, such as wounds or sores. This meant guidance was not always available to support staff to identify concerns and to outline escalation pathways. Despite this, we found no evidence of infection concerns not being highlighted or addressed.

Staff told us, “Care plans we read through and from there we can form a plan to care following the instructions.” However, several care plans lacked the personalised guidance needed to keep people safe. For example, where a person was at risk of choking, there was not sufficient guidance to enable staff to consistently support the person safely. The person had raised concerns about their food not being cut small enough during a recent care review, but this had not resulted in the guidance in their care plan being made clearer for staff to follow. This placed the person at continued risk of harm. The provider took immediate action to update the person’s records during the assessment.

Where people had specific health conditions or needs which could impact on many areas of their care, such as Parkinson’s Disease, this had not always been risk assessed, and guidance was not always in place for staff to support this. The provider addressed these concerns following the assessment.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to not always have a proactive and positive culture of safety. Staff did not always listen to concerns about safety and did not always investigate and report safety events. Lessons were not always learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.

Learning had not always been consistently applied across the service. While staff gave examples of learning following incidents or accidents, we found some incidents had occurred which had not been fully reviewed to ensure learning translated into improved practice. For example, some risk assessments and care plans had not been reviewed following incidents, and the service had missed opportunities to make changes to people’s care to prevent future recurrence. At the time of our assessment, we found the incidents reviewed had been isolated, and people had not experienced repeated issues. The provider made changes to their processes for monitoring and reviewing incidents and accidents, following the concerns raised by the inspector, to ensure safer future practice. We will check this at our next assessment.

Staff described how management shared updates, and 1 staff member told us, “My manager listens and always tries to help.” Staff meetings were used to discuss improvements, but gaps remained in how lessons were monitored and followed through.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to not always make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences.

We found a repeated issue, where the provider had not followed their own Medicine Policy, as medicines were being administered without a Medicine Administration Record (MAR) in place. The provider contacted staff to ensure there were no further incidents of this and put MAR charts in place when this was raised by the inspector.

Some people who were prescribed pain relief patches were not having these administered, with the required number of rotations, in line with the manufacturer’s guidelines. This is important to reduce the risk of skin irritation. The provider updated the guidance following the assessment to ensure staff would be prompted to make the correct number of rotations.

The service had experienced some stock issues, and although the service policy stated they were not responsible for the stock of medicine, staff were responsible for administering people’s medicines as prescribed. There had not always been prompt escalation by staff for medicine stock issues, and some people had missed some of their medicines for short periods of time.

However, there had been some improvement in the way medicines were managed. There was now sufficient guidance for staff in relation to how to administer people’s prescribed creams. The provider's policy had been updated to better reflect the practice they expected from their staff. Feedback from people was now positive about how their medicines were managed. A person said, “The carers always make sure we get our tablets each day.” Staff told us they received training to administer people’s medicines. A staff member told us, “I record on the MAR chart…I would also record if people refused.” Another said, “I check the MAR chart, and we use a no touch policy. We put it into a medication pot and check the name of the person, using the right route, at the right time. I also make sure I log medicine administration in the daily log."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff however they had not always ensured they were suitably deployed to meet people’s needs in line with their preferences. They did not always make sure staff received effective support, supervision and development.

The provider had enough staff employed to cover the care hours they needed to deliver. However, staffing arrangements were not consistently effective. Most calls now start on time or within the accepted half hour variation. However, some calls did not last for the full duration of the call time. Not all staff were given travel time between their care calls, and some staff described pressures in some areas they covered. A staff member said, “Sometimes we don’t get enough travel time.” Another said, “It depends if the next person is close, then it is fine.” When we raised this with the provider, they told us they had identified these areas for improvement and were actively monitoring staff call time performance data and addressing concerns, as well as actively recruiting staff who could more easily cover certain areas.

The data we reviewed in relation to the services call scheduling also showed high variation in staff attending double-up calls. Some people commented that staff consistency could be improved.

Staff were recruited safely with appropriate pre-employment checks completed, including references and Disclosure and Barring Service checks. New staff received an induction, which they told us was informative. A staff member said, “It was really very smooth. I have a good manager, we did training and I shadowed people it was very helpful. When they were happy that I was ok, they left me start work.”

Staff were content with the training they had received. However, some people requested that staff complete training in relation to their specific care needs, which had not been actioned in a timely manner. Training compliance prior to the assessment had not been consistent with some areas of low completion, such as Parkinson’s disease and diabetes awareness. However, during the assessment, the provider significantly increased the training compliance and updated their processes to include more frequent oversight in this area.

At the time of the assessment, the service was behind on staff supervision. The provider was working on getting them up to date. However, staff told us they felt supported in their roles. A staff member said, “They provide guidance and support."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. They did not always make sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Some environmental risks had not been assessed, such as the use of bedrails. During the assessment, we raised with the provider that there were no risk assessments for people who had bedrails in place. The provider investigated the concerns and identified that some people with bedrails did not have protective bumpers in place. They took action to make referral requests for protective bumpers and put relevant risk assessments in place.

Other equipment, such as hoists and stand aids were used appropriately. Staff told us, “Moving and handling someone, I ensure that I follow the procedure and if we need to hoist a person, I follow the procedure. I am not allowed to use the hoist on my own. Ensure the person is comfortable, they are well positioned, ensure all equipment is correct, and batteries are working.” A person told us, “They always check everything before they use it.” Staff had assessed other environmental risks for both people and the staff attending people’s care calls, including risks in people’s home environments and the risk of fire.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to work with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care when people moved between different services.

People’s needs were assessed by senior staff prior to their package of care commencing, and risk assessments and care plans were put in place at the start of their care. A staff member told us, “I do assessments. We look at referrals from the council, and then we assess and speak to people.”

People told us their care was delivered safely day-to-day, and staff understood how to support people with known risks. A relative said, “They are all so kind, caring and very helpful doing all that is needed to make our lives more bearable… When things change with [person’s] condition, we discuss it together and [person’s] care plan is altered accordingly so each of the carers knows what to do.”

Where people required support from other health or social care professionals, the service made appropriate referrals and worked in partnership to meet people’s needs, for example to occupational therapists and district nurses.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to work with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

People told us they felt safe with staff, with 1 person saying, “I feel very safe, the carers all know what to do for me.” People and relatives told us they trusted the staff and felt concerns would be acted on.

Staff had completed safeguarding training. They understood safeguarding and were confident to report concerns. A staff member said, “Safeguarding is making sure a person is safe from harm. I always use it in my role.” Another staff member said, “I have raised a safeguarding. I raised with my manager. I have also raised it with the council and CQC. I did receive feedback and it was dealt with thoroughly.” Safeguarding referrals were discussed during management meetings to ensure any actions and follow up were completed as required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service was in continued breach of legal regulation in relation to governance at the service.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Although leaders understood the context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. Leaders did not always have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. This meant they did not always embody the culture and values of their workforce and organisation.

During the assessment, the nominated individual for the service changed. This change was to strengthen the leadership with greater input into the service. There had also been a newly appointed deputy manager with the aim of distributing the workload and allowing for more in-depth and timely oversight going forward. The newly appointed leadership team had begun developing a governance structure, strengthening audits and allocating clearer responsibilities for oversight. While these new steps showed potential for improvement, they were not yet sufficiently embedded to assure that the service could consistently identify and manage risks moving forward. We will check this at our next assessment.

However, leaders were described by staff as supportive and approachable, and people told us they felt able to raise issues or ask for help. A staff member told us, “[Manager] is very supportive… she gives a listening ear to us.” Another staff member said, “[The registered manager] communicates as much as possible.” This showed that leadership was caring but had not been sufficiently capable or organised to drive and sustain the required improvements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

Most people and relatives told us they had not raised any concerns or made any complaints regarding the service. A person and another person’s relative told us they raised concerns about staff using their mobile phones, which the service dealt with.

Staff told us they felt able to speak up, and they were confident that concerns would be taken seriously. They described an open environment where issues could be raised during team meetings or directly with the manager. A staff member said, “Yes, I can voice my concerns openly, and they do listen.” Another staff member explained that leaders encouraged staff to contribute ideas during meetings. This demonstrated a positive Freedom to Speak Up culture where staff felt valued and supported to contribute to improvements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had not had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They had not acted on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes.

The governance arrangements in some areas remained inconsistent and had not been fully effective in identifying or addressing ongoing risks and oversight. There was no evidence of audits of risk assessments and care plans to identify the gaps in care records we found at this assessment. The registered manager and the previous nominated individual told us they had checked people’s care records, but there were no records to demonstrate this. During the assessment, we raised serious concerns about this practice. The new nominated individual updated the auditing tools to better support staff in identifying areas for improvement and planned to increase the frequency of audits. This began during our assessment however, the changes required time to embed. We will check this at our next assessment.

Medicine audits had failed to identify the concerns we found, such as pain patches not being rotated in line with the manufacturer’s guidelines and medicines being administered without Medicine Administration Records. These issues had been raised at previous assessments and had still not been fully resolved. The provider took immediate action to correct these issues during the assessment; they made changes to the audit template to prompt staff to carry out more in-depth reviews and cross-checking. These improvements needed to be embedded; we will check this at the next assessment.

There had been some improvement to areas of governance since the last assessment such as governance around people’s care call monitoring and an increase in governance meetings to review practice at the service for areas which required improvement, patterns and trends as well as good practice. However, this required further development as the review of accidents and incidents had not identified where sufficient action had not been taken to mitigate future risks. We will check these at the next assessment.

People’s risk assessments and care plans for some needs had improved. For example, around catheter care and moving and handling support. The provider had focused on re-writing people’s care records and 91% of people’s records had been completed. Further work was needed to ensure more timely action was taken to address concerns in relation to people’s care planning and improve governance and oversight across the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had not always focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across all areas of the organisation. They had not always encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They had not always actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.

Although the service had improved in some areas of practice, which they had prioritised since the last assessment, improvements to the service had not been timely. A staff member told us, “Training has changed and we have improved looking at risk assessments and checking care plans to see if there are any problems. An inspection inspired the change, and new technology has also come along.”

However, the service had not consistently learned from previous assessments; some of the same concerns around medicines management and governance had not been fully addressed, and further work was needed. Patterns and trends had been reviewed by the management team each month, but did not reflect on whether there were patterns and trends following previous months.

Before the assessment, a new deputy manager had been appointed but had not yet started at the service. During the assessment, the deputy manager began in post, and there was a change of nominated individual to give more presence and oversight at the service. New governance tools and processes were created during the assessment to strengthen governance and quality assurance systems and processes. These had not yet been implemented long enough to demonstrate enough sustained impact.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider continued to understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

Staff described positive relationships with external professionals, including occupational therapists, district nurses and local authority colleagues. A staff member told us, “We work well with Medway Council… Occupational therapy is very responsive.” Staff gave examples of seeking advice from district nurses regarding pressure care or catheter issues. Relatives and people receiving care also said staff supported them to access healthcare services when needed, and records showed appropriate referrals and follow‑up. This meant the service worked in a joined‑up way to support people’s health and wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider’s culture and direction for the service had not always embedded into the practices within the service. Despite this, the provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture which was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement.

While the cultural values of compassion and person‑centred care were evident, this had not yet translated into consistently safe or robust governance systems. Since the last assessment, the provider had worked with external consultants and introduced new audits however, these changes had not always been timely or effectively implemented. This showed that the provider’s vision for high‑quality, well‑organised care was not consistently embedded and demonstrated that the service had a partially shared direction and culture.

Staff described a positive, caring ethos, and several spoke warmly about the commitment within the team. For example, staff said, “My manager is amazing. She is very approachable; she does listen and always tries to help,” and “[The registered manager] shows concern about you and people we support.” Staff described enjoying their work and wanting the best for the people they supported. People receiving care also consistently spoke about the kindness of the staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

Staff described being treated fairly and being supported with personal needs where necessary. A staff member told us, “[The manager] adjusts the rota if we have a personal emergency.” Other staff explained they felt respected and encouraged in their roles. There was no evidence of discriminatory practice, and staff confirmed that training and development opportunities were accessible to all. This contributed to a sense of inclusion and fairness across the workforce.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
