asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for London Care (Rochester)
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
We carried out this comprehensive assessment between 2 and 18 July 2025. London Care (Rochester) is a domiciliary care agency providing personal care to people in the community in their own houses and flats. At the time of this inspection, they were providing personal care to 237 people and two of the people they supported had a learning disability. We assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted.

We announced the site visit to the provider 48 hours beforehand; this was because we needed to be sure there would be a manager available to support this inspection.

We spoke with 11 people who used the service, 10 relatives, 11 staff members, a manager, regional manager, care director and the head of quality assurance. We received feedback from 1 professional involved in the service. We reviewed 20 people’s care records, staff records and records relating to the management of the service.

The provider was previously in breach of the 3 legal regulations in relation to safe care and treatment, personal centred care and good governance. At this inspection, improvements had not been made, and the provider remained in breach of 3 regulations in relation to good governance, safe care and treatment and person-centred care. The provider continued to fail to have effective systems in place to identify, monitor and manage risks for people. Care plans failed to address people’s individual needs in relation to their physical health and emotional needs, and the provider failed to address shortfalls in the service promptly to ensure it was effective and safe.

Risks to people’s health and well-being were not thoroughly assessed and managed in a way that reduced the likelihood of harm to them. Care was not always planned and delivered in a person-centred manner.

The management team were not proactive in ensuring that shortfalls identified in the service were addressed and action plans implemented promptly.
Staff were deployed to meet people’s needs. People told us they received their scheduled care visits at the right time to meet their needs. There were no missed visits recorded. Recruitment checks were completed as required to keep people safe. The administration and management of people’s medicines was safe. Staff told us, and records showed that staff had completed training relevant to their roles and were supported to improve their performance. Complaints and concerns were investigated and managed in line with the provider’s procedure.

We have asked the provider for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is not performing as well as it should and we have told the service how it must improve.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People and their relatives told us they felt safe with staff and that staff treated them with respect and dignity. They commented that staff were kind and caring. People told us staff completed their care visits as agreed. Staff gave people choice and promoted their independence.

People told us staff obtained consent from them and respected their choices. People knew how to express their views about the service but complained that the office and management staff were not always accessible and responsive. They commented that phone calls were not answered, and calls were not returned.

People felt concerned that the service did not always notify them about changes in their care, and when there were changes to their regular care staff.

People felt the service was not well and effectively run.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant people did not always feel well-supported, cared for or treated with dignity and respect.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care. It did not consistently consider individuals’ emotional wellbeing, the factors contributing to their distress, or the support they needed.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always caring

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider promoted people’s independence, so people knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing. One person told us, “I feel much more independent, the carers enable me to do what I can do while they get on with other things like cooking and cleaning.” One relative stated that, “The main carer always encourages [person] to do what they can do for themselves. When they are moving from one chair to another, the carer stands back to give them space but will be there to help if needed. The carer encourages them but never bosses them about.”

Care plans outlined individual’s abilities and highlighted where they required assistance. Staff described how they promoted people’s autonomy by allowing people to choose how their daily care was provided. One staff member mentioned, “I offer people choices and promote independence by trying to get them to help with things. I would let them choose what they would like to wear and how they want to be washed, and choices of food.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always treat people with kindness, empathy and compassion, or respect their privacy and dignity. Staff did not always treat colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect.

One person told us, “I think the carers have a good personality. We are always having a chat from the time they arrive to the time they leave. They are very caring in all areas.” Another person mentioned, “Most of the carers who come are quite friendly and my regular carer is a nice person. They understand that this is my home, and they respect my home too. They ask my permission before they do anything, and they always give me a choice.”

Whilst we received positive feedback from people about how caring and kind staff were, we also received comments that not all staff were compassionate and kind. One person commented, “There is one staff that just gets on with what they are doing without communicating much or thinking about what they are doing and how it might make me feel. They focus on the job and that makes me feel very anxious.” People told us staff discussed other people’s matters in front of them and they were worried their personal matter would also be discussed with others without consideration for confidentiality.

One relative stated, “There is a massive difference with other carers, for example; other carers will not wash my relative properly and just hand them a flannel with cold water without any thought or consideration and virtually no communication.” Another relative mentioned, “Some carers offer no warmth or kindness. It’s just about the job and not the person.”

Staff had received training and induction on the core principles of care which included respecting people’s dignity and privacy. Staff gave us examples how they promoted these values in their day-to-day work.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always listen to or understand people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff did not always respond to people’s needs in the moment or act to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.

Care plans included observations on individuals’ behaviours and emotional needs but lacked insight into potential triggers for changes in mood or behaviour. Two care plans identified individuals living with anxiety yet failed to detail what might cause them stress or offer guidance to help staff recognise when they were anxious or distressed. Similar gaps were found in the care plans of people experiencing depression. For example, there were no indicators to help staff identify early signs of low mood or emotional decline. We were concerned that without this crucial information, staff may struggle to recognise when someone needs emotional support or is in distress, limiting their ability to respond appropriately.

People and their relatives expressed concerns that emotional needs were not considered when planning staff rotas. One person shared, “I feel very anxious when I don’t know who’s coming. It worries me and makes me upset. I’ve mentioned it before, but they don’t always inform me when a new carer will arrive, they just show up.”

A relative commented, “My [relative] has dementia, and different carers visit each day. I understand consistency isn’t always possible, but efforts should be made to minimise disruption. They also frequently change visit times without notifying us, which is particularly distressing for someone with dementia.” Another relative stated, “We don’t receive any kind of rota. As a result, my [relative] lacks a consistent routine and has become resistant to accepting help. It’s not right to keep sending unfamiliar carers to someone with dementia.” A third added, “My relative doesn’t always feel safe or comfortable with the carers. They don’t know who these people are and feel frightened.” This meant that the provider had failed to ensure people’s immediate and emotional needs were always planned and met in a person-centred way.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

Staff understood and promoted equality and diversity amongst people. One staff member told us, “I take into account people’s religious and cultural requirements when supporting them and adapt the way I care for them to meet their specific needs.”

Records indicated people’s protected characteristics such as religion, culture, gender, sexuality, disability and race were covered as part of their needs assessment. Where people required support to attend places of worship, staff supported them. People were addressed by their preferred names and titles, and people’s preference as to the gender of staff to deliver their care was respected.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff and supported.

Staff told us their well-being was promoted. They told us they had regular contacts with their supervisors to check they were doing well and if they had any concerns. They told us they felt supported in their roles through training and supervisions. Staff felt motivated to continue delivering effective care to people. One staff told us how they had been supported to improve in their role and how the provider had recognised their commitment and hard work. Another member of staff told us the provider had been very supportive and offered them flexibility so they could continue to balance work and their other commitments.

The provider had various programmes to support staff’s wellbeing including regular wellbeing checks, supervisions, reward events, and employee assistance programme which all staff had access to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant the effectiveness of people’s care, treatment and support did not always achieve good outcomes or was inconsistent.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care. Care plans were not person-centred to show how people’s health and emotional needs would be met.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always effective

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

Care records contained information about people’s physical and mental health condition, personal care, medication, nutritional and skin care needs. However, information about people’s needs were not comprehensive and detailed to ensure staff knew how to support people’s needs to keep them healthy and safe. For example, two care records stated the people had a learning disability. The Right support, right care, right culture (RSRCRC) model should be used when assessing the needs of people with learning disabilities. However, no details had been provided on the nature or type of learning disability they had, how it impacted on them, and how they should be supported to maximise their well-being. As already stated, we also found that some people’s care needs assessments did not provide sufficient details about their physical health conditions and how they needed to be supported to keep them safe and well.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

People consented to their care and support before it was delivered. The manager understood their roles and responsibilities under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). They had assessed people’s mental capacity to make specific decisions where they had concerns about the person’s capacity.

People’s capacity was documented in their care plans. Where they received support to make decisions it was also documented and who supported them with such decisions. Where people had Court of Protection orders or lasting powers of attorney, they were noted in their care plans.

Staff had received training in MCA, and they knew the importance of gaining people’s consent in relation to the care and support they received.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

People were supported with their nutritional needs. One person told us, “They make me some cereal or toast for breakfast and at lunchtime they reheat a meal for me and leave me with a drink. I tell them what I want.” Care plans detailed what support people needed to shop for food, prepare their meals and if they had any special diets or nutritional requirements. One person was supported to have fortified drinks. Staff told us if they had concerns with people’s eating and drinking, they reported this to their manager so that appropriate support would be provided. Staff told us they left water within reach for people and encouraged them to drink especially during hot weather.

Staff were trained and supported to recognise concerns with people’s nutrition and how to support them appropriately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services.

Staff liaised and shared information about people, their relatives where appropriate and other agencies involved in the person’s care. For example, if people needed to go to hospital, they gave them a copy of their care plan or care passport which contained important information about them.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not always ensure that outcomes were positive and

consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

The manager told us they used monitoring visits and reviews to assess the outcome people received from the care provided to improve their experience. However, people told their monitoring checks did not always improve outcomes for them. One person told us, “Every now and then I might get a phone call asking about what I think of the carers. But they are very brief questions, and nothing ever improves with my feedback. I have mentioned to them about informing me when they change my regular carer or when they change the times, but it hasn't really improved.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.

People were supported to access a range of health and social care services as needed. Records showed a range of health and social care services were involved to maintain people’s health and well-being. For example, staff had contact details for community nurses who looked after people’s catheter. Staff told us they contacted people’s GP if they needed support to arrange medical appointments.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant people’s needs were not always met.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care. Care plans were not tailored to people’s individual needs.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always responsive

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There were some shortfalls in how the provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was not always joined-up, flexible or supportive of choice and continuity.

The service supported people with learning disabilities. Their care plans failed to address how their individual needs would be met in line with The Right support, right care, right culture (RSRCRC) model, and lacked detail about how to work effectively with other health care professionals to meet their bespoke needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it. People’s care packages were planned in advance and agreed with people, their relatives and the referring authority. Care plans detailed people’s preferences to care visit times, tasks to be completed and how to carry out those tasks. However, people reported that the service was not always flexible and accommodating to changes in visit times. One person told us, “I have requested for my time to be adjusted but this has not happened.”

The provider had an 'Out of Hours' procedure in place, which was communicated to both individuals receiving care and staff, enabling contact with the office outside of standard working hours. Despite this, several people reported challenges in accessing support during both regular and out-of-hours periods. One individual shared, “We can’t always reach them when we need to. Sometimes I’d like an early evening visit or a later one, but I can’t speak to anyone about it.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.

Care plans included information about people’s religion, race, gender and other protected characteristics. Staff had completed training in equality and diversity. They told us they respected people as individuals irrespective of their backgrounds, religious, culture and other protected characteristics.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff did not always involve people in decisions about their care or tell them what had changed as a result.

People and their relatives told us they would contact the office to raise their complaint or concerns about the service. However, they mentioned that it was very difficult to get hold of a member of the management team on the phone if they needed to express their dissatisfaction. One person stated, “It’s almost impossible to get hold of the manager or any office staff when you want them. You leave a message, and you never get a call back.”

The provider had a complaints procedure which they followed. A log was kept of all complaints received, detailing actions taken and any lessons learned.
Over the past six months, a pattern had emerged from a review of the complaints that highlighted a concern about the quality of care people received. In response, the provider stated they were actively exploring training opportunities to help staff enhance their performance and improve service standards.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not always work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any changes in people’s individual needs.

Care plans lacked personalisation and were not tailored to the specific needs of people. While care records listed medical and physical health conditions, including accompanying information sheets, there were no individualised plans to guide staff in delivering appropriate support. Care plans for people with diabetes, epilepsy, and respiratory conditions revealed an absence of detail on how staff should assist people effectively with these conditions. Similarly, care plans for two individuals with dementia and two others experiencing depression and anxiety offered no insight into how these conditions impacted them or how support should be adapted accordingly. For two individuals with a learning disability, there was no information on the nature of their condition, its effects, or tailored support approaches to meet their individual needs. Additionally, care plans failed to outline any emotional support needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.

There was no one receiving end of life care at the time of our visit. The manager told us they would work with people’s relatives, other health professionals and services to support people if they required this service. Staff had received end of life care training.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.

People’s care plans included their communication needs and how best to achieve effective communication. For example, when a person’s first language was not English, they would require an interpreter to translate for them, or if people preferred information shared with them in another way such as easy read or pictorial formats. The provider told us they would provide information available in different languages, and formats if people needed this.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant some aspects of the service were not always safe and there was limited assurance about safety. There was an increased risk that people could be harmed.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safe care and treatment. Risks to people’s health was not assessed and no mitigations had been put in place to reduce harm.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always safe

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.

People were protected from the spread of infection. People and their relatives told us staff followed infection control procedures to prevent infection and contamination. One person commented, “They all wear the aprons and gloves when they are washing me.” Another person mentioned, “They seem to have very satisfactory hygiene standards”. “They keep me clean and the environment clean. They wear the protective clothing and gloves.”

Staff confirmed that had received training in infection control. The provider provided personal protective equipment (PPE) for staff use. Staff understood their responsibilities in ensuring the risk of infection was reduced. They told us they washed their hands effectively and used PPE appropriately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage their individual risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. For example, some people commented that staff did not always make them feel safe by involving them in the task they are doing. One person commented, “There is one staff that just gets on with what they are doing without communicating much or thinking about what they are doing and how they are doing it. It makes me feel very much unsafe.”

However, some people told us they felt safe in the way staff supported them. One person said, “They help me to shower and to get dressed and they always chat with me as they are helping me. I feel safe that way.” Another person commented, “I have an equipment installed by the occupational therapy team. They help me use it safely.”

Whilst we found risk assessments to support people in areas such as mobility, pressure sores, and personal care; risks associated with people’s physical health were not robust and there was no management plan in place to promote the individual’s safety and well-being. For example, there was no risk assessment and guidance for one individual with epilepsy to help staff identify when the person had a seizure and how to respond to keep them safe. There was also a lack of detail about how to identify and respond to the risks regarding four individuals who had diabetes. Two individuals had been identified as having recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) in their care records. However, no risk assessment had been conducted to determine the underlying causes or to implement preventative measures aimed at reducing the likelihood of future occurrences for these individuals. Another individual had a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. However, the associated risks had not been assessed, and no management plan was in place to mitigate these risks or ensure safe and appropriate support.

We raised our concerns with the provider during our feedback session, and they completed a risk assessment for the individuals we had identified.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider was not always proactive in addressing and ensuring learning from incidents, accidents and when things go wrong. Staff knew how to report incidents and accidents. They told us they sometimes had to remind their managers to follow up on concerns they had raised, and the managers did not always feedback to them regarding the outcomes of their investigations and did not always share learning from them. One staff member said, “I report any concerns on the record book. I also let the manager know but we don’t always get told what they have done about it.”

We noted that there had not been a consistent approach to sharing learning from incidents and when things go wrong. While we saw that most incidents noted actions taken to address most recent incidents, there was not always evidence to show they had been shared with staff to improve their learning and experiences.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. Staff involved people in planning, including when changes happened.

The provider had a medicine administration and management policy in place which staff followed. Staff had completed training in the safe administration and management of medicines.
People had care plans in place which included details about the level of support they received with managing their medicines such as ordering and who supported them. Care plans also included a list of people’s medicines and how they were taken. Medicine Administration Records (MAR) charts were maintained to show when medicines had been administered as prescribed. MAR charts were signed and dated. People told us they received their medicines as required. Staff knew what actions to take if they had concerns about people’s medicines.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.

People and their relatives were mostly satisfied with staff attendance and punctuality. They told us staff arrived at the scheduled time most of the time. One person said, “They send two carers on each visit to us. The carers usually arrive at about the same time. They have never not turned up.” Another person told us, “I have two carers, one in the morning and one in the evening”. “The carers turn up on time and very reliable.” However, some people commented that staff were sometimes late, and they were not always notified of this. For example, one person stated, “They are often late or sometimes they don't turn up at all.” Another person commented, “The carers don’t always turn up on time. They can be late for up to two hours.”

The service used an electronic monitoring system (ECM) to plan and monitor care visits. Analysis of the ECM data showed 87% of calls were delivered within 15 minutes of the planned time and doubled handed visits were completed by 2 members of staff. There were no missed visits recorded.

Planned and unplanned absences were covered by staff who were willing to do extra hours. The care coordinator told us they matched staff to people looking at skills, availability and location to ensure people’s needs were met.

Training records showed and staff told us they felt supported in their roles. They told us they received an induction when they started and had received the training, they needed to be effective in their roles. One staff member commented, “I shadowed for one week and they assessed me as competent to do the job. I get regular supervisions and well-being checks. I understand the job now.”

The provider followed safe recruitment processes to ensure people were supported by staff who were fit and suitable to support them. Recruitment records included satisfactory references, right to work in the UK, employment history, and criminal records checks.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.

Staff conducted a risk assessment of people’s home environments where care was delivered to ensure it was safe for people and staff. The assessment looks at the physical environment including access to the property, fire and electrical risks and equipment used for the delivery of care. Care plans reminded staff to always do a visual check of the environment and equipment before delivering care and to report any concerns.

The service kept a record of maintenance and checks completed on equipment used for people’s care such as moving and handling equipment and transfer aids. This reduced the risk of harm from faulty and unsafe equipment.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety. They did not make sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.

The provider had a team of staff who screened referrals to make sure they were suitable for the service. They reviewed the care needs assessments completed by the referring authority to understands the individual’s needs. The manager told us they contacted people to discuss their preferences around the times of visits and the start date. They told us they sent experienced care staff to do people’s first care visits, and they used this opportunity to assess and confirm people’s needs. Whilst the manager told us this system works well for the service, staff told us they found this system difficult as they did not always know people’s needs before visiting them. One staff commented, “We often arrive at clients’ homes without knowing what to expect, as new clients are not always assessed prior to the start of care. This means we often begin supporting the person without a clear understanding of their needs or how best to assist them.” Another staff member told us, “Discussing a service user's needs while actively delivering care is not ideal. It's important to have a dedicated conversation beforehand taking the time to sit down with them and understand their preferences and expectations for how care should be provided. Too often, we enter someone's home for the first time without any prior insight, which can leave both the carer and the individual feeling unsafe.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately.

People told us they felt safe with staff in their home. One person commented, “I’m not worried about my safety in the presence of the carers.” Another person mentioned, “I’m feeling safe, and I like the carers I’m getting at the moment.”

Staff told us and training record showed staff had been trained in safeguarding adults from abuse. Staff knew what actions to take to safeguard people from abuse. One staff member told us, “I will report it straight away to the manager. If the manager is not available, then I would email the manager or call the next person in line.” Another staff member stated, “You must report [safeguarding concerns]. I would contact the office. You can also contact other people like CQC or someone else.”

The manager knew their responsibilities to safeguard people. They told us they would follow their procedures and work closely with the local authority safeguarding team to investigate and deal with any safeguarding concerns.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question requires improvement. At this assessment the rating has remained requires improvement.

This meant the management and leadership was inconsistent. Leaders and the culture they created did not always support the delivery of high-quality, person-centred care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance. The provider did not take timely action to rectify gaps in the service, compromising its effectiveness and safety.
keyQuestionRatings.narrative: This service is not always well-led

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Not all leaders understood the context in which the provider delivered care, treatment and support. They did not always embody the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders did not always have the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively, or they did not always do so with integrity, openness and honesty.

The service had a manager who was undergoing the process to become the registered manager for the service. They were supported in their role by the regional manager, head of quality and homecare director. At the time of our visit, they were the registered manager for two other services, and they shared their time supporting all three services. They informed us that the provider intended to assign them responsibility solely for managing the London Care Rochester location. We were concerned that at the current time the manager may lack the capacity to manage all three services effectively and safely. People using the service reported that they did know who the manager was. A recurring theme from people’s feedback was the absence of clear managerial identity and communication, with people and relatives stating, “I don’t know who the manager is or who runs the office,' and 'It’s quite hard to get through to the office anyway.”

Staff knew who to contact if they needed support. They told us they had regular support from the field supervisors and care coordinators who were involved in the day-to-day operations of the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

The provider actively promoted a Freedom to Speak Up policy, fostering an environment where staff felt empowered to voice concerns. A clear system was in place that allowed employees to raise issues with any manager across the organisation. This culture of openness encouraged staff to speak up about anything they had witnessed or heard.

Both staff and service users understood how to report concerns, whether internally or to external bodies, and felt confident to do so. One staff member shared, “The company has a strong communication system. We all have an app on our phones that lets us contact anyone in the organisation. They really encourage open and direct communication. I usually raise concerns with the branch manager, then escalate if needed.” Another added, “I’m not afraid to speak up. If I have concerns, I’d go to the manager or senior manager, and if necessary, contact external organisations like the CQC or local authority.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate.

Although the provider had implemented a range of systems and procedures to assess and oversee the quality of the service, these mechanisms were not consistently effective in identifying issues or initiating actions to drive meaningful improvements. These processes included conducting staff spot checks, auditing care documentation, medication administration records, training logs, recruitment files, incident and accident reports, safeguarding records, and complaints.

At a regional level, the service was also monitored by the director, who reviewed incidents and accidents, complaints, safeguarding concerns, survey feedback, and overall service performance. Where necessary, they established actions to support improvement.

However, during this inspection, we found shortcomings in the care records. Care plans lacked sufficient detail and failed to accurately reflect the risks associated with individuals’ health conditions, their specific needs, or the strategies required to manage those risks. Although the provider had acknowledged these deficiencies in their current improvement plan, the issues identified during this visit were consistent with those raised in the previous inspection in 2019.

The provider informed us that they were in the process of reviewing all care plans using a newly introduced system. Following our inspection, they had updated the specific care plans where concerns had been identified.

Feedback from individuals and their relatives indicated concerns regarding the effectiveness of the service’s management. Comments from people and relatives reflected dissatisfaction with leadership visibility, communication, and responsiveness. For example, one person remarked, 'I would not recommend London Care as a whole, with the only exception being the regular carers.' Another stated, 'I would score the management 6 out of 10.' Several individuals expressed frustration at the lack of managerial presence, noting that leaders appeared disconnected from frontline operations and were difficult to reach by phone. One person commented, 'They need to get out a bit more and see what happens on the floor instead of sitting in the office. You also can’t get hold of them when you call.'' Concerns were also raised about the office’s customer service, with multiple reports of unanswered calls, and failure to return messages.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not always encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They did not always actively contribute to safe, effective practice and research.

The provider had a service improvement plan outlining their strategies for enhancing and developing the service. For instance, the quality manager mentioned plans to recruit a dedicated staff member to oversee the electronic call monitoring system. However, progress in implementing these improvements had been slow. Several issues identified during this inspection mirrored those found in the previous one, indicating limited improvement.

The manager was part of the provider’s wider network of managers and shared that they regularly exchanged ideas and best practices aimed at improving service delivery.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.

The provider worked in partnership with a wide range of organisations to improve the service delivered to people and to ensure people’s needs were met. They liaised with local authorities, health and social care services, day services providers and other agencies to develop and meet the needs of people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Not all staff consistently upheld the provider’s vision, strategic direction, and organisational culture. The provider actively facilitated both local and corporate initiatives, such as roadshows, annual award ceremonies and newsletters, to communicate and reinforce its values and objectives. Staff reported receiving an employee handbook upon commencement of employment and confirmed that the induction programme covered the provider’s ethos and aims which emphasised providing high quality and compassion.

Staff demonstrated an understanding of the organisation’s core values; however, concerns were raised that not all staff consistently adhered to these principles. It was further noted that the management team did not conduct regular spot checks to monitor staff performance and conduct. These concerns were echoed by people and their relatives, who reported variability in the level of care provided, with some staff perceived as more compassionate and compliant with procedures than others. For instance, people highlighted that not all staff, including office staff, always informed them when staff were running late for scheduled visits. Additionally, there were complaints regarding the quality of customer service from office staff, who were said to frequently neglect responding to messages or returning phone calls.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.

A staff member shared their appreciation for the organisation’s flexibility, explaining that due to personal commitments, they were only available to work part-time on specific days. The organisation accommodated their needs, which they found incredibly supportive.

Training records indicated that staff had completed courses in equality and diversity. The provider actively promoted inclusivity through its recruitment practices, offering tailored support to staff with language barriers or disabilities to ensure successful completion of training and induction programs.

Both the manager and quality manager described various initiatives and events designed to foster team building and enhance workplace collaboration.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
