asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Optimum Supported Housing Limited
asgRatings.name: Supported Living
asgRatings.commentary:
We completed an inspection between 30 June 2025 and 04 July 2025. Optimum supported Housing Limited is a supported living service that provides individuals with personal care and support in their own homes or shared accommodation. We assessed the service against ‘Right support, right care, right culture’ guidance to make judgements about whether the provider guaranteed people with a learning disability and autistic people respect, equality, dignity, choices, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. The service was not meeting the guidance of RSRCRC: this had a detrimental impact on people’s lives. There was a closed culture at the service. A "closed culture" is a poor culture that can lead to harm, including human rights breaches and abuse. We found a poor culture across the entire service, which had not been recognised or addressed by the provider.

The provider failed to ensure people’s health risks were well managed, and people were not supported by suitably qualified and competent staff. Medicines had not been managed safely. People were not treated with dignity, kindness and respect. There was a lack of effective oversight of the service to identify and make improvements. Audits and checks that were completed had not identified the serious and widespread issues identified at this inspection. The provider was also the registered manager of the service.

We found significant shortfalls across the service and identified breaches of 7 regulations in relation to providing people with person centred care, safeguarding, safe care and treatment, need for consent, staffing, dignity and respect and good governance.

This service is being placed in special measures. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we user our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a timeframe within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide. In instances where CQC have decided to take civil or criminal enforcement action against a provider, we will publish this information on our website after any representations and/or appeals have been concluded.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing badly and we've taken action against the person or organisation that runs it.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: While people expressed general satisfaction with their care, our assessment found elements of care did not meet the expected standards. For example, people’s health and wellbeing risks were not being well managed. This included people not always being protected from the risk of unlawful restraint.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

This is the first assessment for this service at the new registered address This key question has been rated inadequate. This meant people were not treated with compassion and there were breaches of dignity; staff caring attitudes had significant shortfalls.

The service was in breach of legal regulations in relation to person centred care and dignity and respect.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not ensure that people were consistently supported to have choice and control over their own care and to make decisions about their care, treatment and wellbeing. People’s care and support plans contained very little detail on how staff can support people to be as independent as possible. For example, some people’s care plans did not contain goals that were specific to them. We found that goals were described as ‘future expectations’ which were generic and the same for most people, such as ‘maintain good health and hygiene’. Where ‘future expectations’ had been detailed it was not clear how staff should support the person to achieve these goals and there was no reference to these being reviewed, to assess if they were still relevant or if they had achieved them.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had not ensured that people were consistently treated with kindness, empathy and compassion. Some staff we spoke with did not know people well and did not treat people with compassion. We spoke to one staff member and asked how they would support them when a person was distressed, they told us they would just tell them to stop. This person experienced frequent episodes of distress, and telling the person to ‘stop’ meant they were not treated with compassion, nor did they have their assessed needs met in a safe and supportive way. However, we did speak to one staff member who had a better understanding of how to support people with kindness and compassion. One person we spoke with told us they were happy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always listen to and understand people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff did not always respond to people’s needs in the moment or act to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress. For example, incidents where one person became distressed, it was not documented how staff supported them and what action they took to help support the person safely and in their best interest. When we spoke to staff, they had a poor understanding of what to when the person was distressed. One staff member told us they would hold the persons hands, which is a form of restraint that was not detailed in their care plan. We saw there were occasions where people were supported to access medical assistance via the GP, 111 or 999 if they needed it. Some people’s daily notes document where staff have contacted 111 to ask for advice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People’s individual needs and preferences were not always understood, and they were not always reflected in their care and support. For example, one person’s care plan detailed were of a particular faith, however there was no other information about what is important for them with this faith to ensure staff can be respectful and help support them with their religion.

However, staff did support some people’s personal, cultural, social and religious needs. For example, one person’s care plan detailed ‘I do practice the Christian religion and attend mass on Sundays.’ Whilst there was no other information in the care and support plan, daily notes detailed that on Sundays, the person did attend an online mass.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always care about and promote the wellbeing of their staff. They did not always support or enable staff to deliver person-centred care. We reviewed rotas that the provider shared with us which showed that staff who had a work visa, and should only be working 20 hours per week, were working over this. For example, one person was working 16 hours over their restriction in one week. The provider had not considered the impact on staff’s wellbeing from working a high number of hours each week.

We reviewed minutes from a team meeting held via video in June 2025, but staff wellbeing was not discussed. However, we spoke to some staff who were happy with their role as support worker.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

This is the first assessment for this service at the new registered address. This key question has been rated inadequate. This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in people’s care, support and outcomes.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care and consent.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure people’s care and treatment was effective because they did not check and discuss people’s health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. The provider failed to ensure people needs were fully assessed. One person’s care plan detailed they had a cataract and needed staff support to attend check-ups. There was no other information regarding the person’s cataract, how this affected them on a daily basis, when their last checkup was or when their next appointment was. Assessments of care were not up to date and staff did not understand people’s current needs. One person’s care plan stated ‘[relative] said they have a history of diabetes’. There was no other information in the care plan regarding support that this person may need regarding diabetes.

People’s communication needs were not fully assessed, which meant the effectiveness of their care could not be maximised. One person’s care plan detailed they needed staff to talk in short sentences or British sign language. There was no other guidance in the persons care plan regarding the persons communication needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider failed to ensure that people’s capacity was assessed in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005. There was very limited information in people’s care plans around their capacity. One person’s care plan detailed they ‘lacked capacity to make complex decisions. There was no other information around what type of decisions these were and what happens when complex decisions needed to be made on their behalf.

The provider had failed to ensure capacity assessments that were in place were accurate and appropriate. One person had a capacity assessment regarding accessing the community and that they needed support of 1 staff member. However, the person needed the support of 2 staff member at all times and this was a greater restriction placed upon that person which was not included in the discussion. They also had a capacity assessment regarding their diet but it was not clear what why this capacity assessment was required and what restriction was in place.

We observed at 2 of the locations that the front doors were locked and only staff had access to the key. There was no information in people’s care plans regarding the front door being locked or whether people lacked the capacity and whether the restriction placed on them was in their best interest.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always plan and deliver people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. People’s care and support was not always delivered in-line with best practice guidance. For example, NICE guidance around medicines administration was not followed by staff. The accessible information standard had not been considered by the provider. For example, one person’s care plan detailed they had as speech impairment, however there was very limited information for staff on how they should communicate with this person effectively.

People’s nutritional needs were not fully considered in their care plans. For example, one person’s care plan detailed ‘I do not need staff to prompt me to eat and drink but requires staff support to prepare healthy and balanced diets.’ However, no other information was detailed for staff including what food they did or didn’t like.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always work well across teams and services to support people. They did not always share their assessment of people’s needs when people moved between different services. Staff did not have access to the information they need to appropriately assess, plan and deliver people’s care, treatment and support. For example, people’s support plans did not contain information that was accurate or reflective of people’s current needs. Whilst information in people’s care and support plans were poor, we saw occasions where staff did support people to access other health professionals, such as psychiatrists and the mental health team.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not routinely monitor people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They did not ensure that outcomes were positive and consistent, or that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. The provider did not have systems in place to monitoring and review people’s outcomes. People’s care plans were not reflective of their current needs and risks assessments were not updated following changes in health conditions. For example, one person had seen their GP regarding constipation but the care plan and guidance for staff had not been implemented, neither had a bowel monitoring chart. Staff could not be sure that the person’s health may be deteriorating due to the lack of monitoring in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always support people to manage their health and wellbeing, so people could not always maximise their independence, choice and control. People’s care plans did not document how they are encouraged and supported to make healthier choices to help promote and maintain their health and wellbeing. Staff completed daily notes, but they contained very limited information and did not detail how they have supported people with their health and wellbeing. People’s care plans did not provide detailed guidance to staff around people’s oral health, particularly if there were concerns. For example, one person’s care plan detailed that they needed to spend a longer time brushing their teeth. There was no other information as to why this was the case and if they needed more regularly support from a dentist. However, daily notes for people did detail if they had supported people with their oral healthcare but with the lack of detailed guidance we are not assured staff were supporting them in a way that met their needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.

This is the first assessment for this service at the new registered address This key question has been rated inadequate. This meant services were not planned or delivered in ways that met people’s needs.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to person centred care.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary: There were significant shortfalls in how the provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was not joined-up, flexible or supportive of choice and continuity. People did not always have continuity of care from staff. The provider told us the work force was predominantly agency staff which meant the provider could not assure people there would be consistency with their care and support staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always make sure that people could access the care and support they needed when they needed it. People’s care and support plan did not always provide enough guidance for staff around accessing other service. For example, one person’s care plan said they needed to visit the dentist, but did not document when their last visit to the dentist was, when their next appointment was, if there were any recommendation from the dentist or how the provider will ensure that attending the dentist is made accessible for that person when considering their support needs.

People were supported to access services such a GP practice, but the appointments were not always recorded and documented by staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People’s care and support did not always promote equality or remove barriers and delays. Whilst people told us they were mostly happy with their care they received, people’s care plans did not always ensure staff could support positive outcomes for people. For example, one person with epilepsy had poor guidance in place and staff had a very poor understanding on how to support someone with epilepsy safely and in a positive way where they could access the community without barriers. There was no information in the care and support plan on how to ensure they were able to access to community safely in relation to their epilepsy.

Some people were supported to access places in relation to their protected characteristics, such as religious places.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider had not always ensured that people and relatives could feedback in a range of accessible ways. For example, one person’s first language was not English and there was not detail in their care plan on ways they could make a complaint or how they could be supported to make a complaint in an accessible way of their choosing.

The provider had a complaints policy in place and 1 complaint had been received. Whilst the records detailed that the provider had taken action following the complaint, such as updating care plans and risk assessments, there was no evidence of this. Also, the complaint records detailed that future feedback from the relative needed to be sought. However, there is no record of future feedback being sought or how the provider would ensure this action was followed.

The complaints policy was not in an accessible format for all people. For example, for people who had a cognitive impairment, there was not a picture format complaints policy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not make sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they did not work in partnership with people, to decide how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. The provider failed to ensure people who use services and those close to them (including carers and dependants) are regularly involved in planning and making shared decisions about their care and treatment, so it is centred around them and their needs. For example, we identified 3 people where their care and support plans had not been discussed or agreed with the person or their representative. One person moved into the service in July 2022, and their care plan was not implemented until September 2024. The care plan also did not detail who was involved with forming and approving the care plan.

The provider did not always ensure that care and support plans detailed people’s goals and aspirations, where expectations were detailed, these were generic and not person centred. For example, one person’s ‘future expectation’ around washing was to ‘reduce infection and spread of germs’. Another ‘future expectation’ around a person’s morning routine was to ‘Maintain good health and personal hygiene’. People were not supported to create goals that were personal to them and there was no information for staff to ensure they could support people to meet goals they had.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary: People were not always supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life. People’s care plans did not always contain information around end of life care planning. Where end of life planning was considered for one person, there was very little detail on what was discussed, the outcome of the discussion and who made those decisions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not supply appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. People’s care and support plans were not accurate and did not contain important details around people’s health conditions and what support they need from staff. People’s communication preferences were not always considered. One person’s care plan detailed they needed staff to communicate with them using short sentences or British Sign Language (BSL). There was no other information within the care plan in relation to BSL and how staff should support the person with their communication preference.

One person’s first language was not English, and they required an interpreter to support them to understand decisions being made. Whilst some documents did detail that an interpreter was used there was no other information as to what support the person receives on a day to day basis with their communication.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. This is the first assessment for this service at the new registered address. This key question has been rated Inadequate. This meant people were not safe and were at risk of avoidable harm.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to safeguarding, safe care and treatment and staffing.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always assess or manage the risk of infection. They did not always detect and control the risk of it spreading or share concerns with appropriate agencies promptly. The provider had not ensured that all staff had completed IPC training, some staff were not on the training matrix and therefore we could not be assured that all staff had completed IPC training.

Information in people’s care plans was basic around IPC and did not contain detailed information for staff on how to support people with risks relating to IPC. For example, one person’s care plan detailed they needed 1-1 support with cleaning products, but there was no other information.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. The provider had not ensured risks to people’s health were well managed and there was a lack of effective guidance in place to inform staff how to support people safely. For example, some people were at risk of constipation and there was no guidance in place for staff to follow to ensure staff could support people to manage this and seek medical assistance if required. People who had epilepsy did not have effective care and support plans in place. There was a lack of information for staff to follow regarding seizures and how to support people if they had a seizure either in their home or in the community. In addition, staff we spoke with did not have the knowledge to support people safely with epilepsy. People who needed support when they were anxious or distressed did not have effective guidance in place for staff. For example, 1 person could get anxious during personal care and display physical behaviours towards staff. However, there was no information in their care plan to guide staff on how to support them. One person had been diagnosed with multiple mental health disorders. There was no information or guidance in their care plan on how staff could support the person on a day to day basis or if they reached a mental health crisis.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not have a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. The provider did not have a robust system in place to review incidents and accidents and ensure appropriate action was taken. The incident log detailed one person had a fall in February 2025, but the exact date was recorded as unknown. The actions detailed ‘add additional measures to keep them safe’. There was no other information as to what these additional measures were and how this would be monitored. Leaders had not reviewed the person’s daily notes and had not spoken to staff to gain an account of the incident. Another incident was recorded on 25 April 2025 where a person was very unwell and vomiting. This had not been reviewed by the provider and no other information was detailed as to what medical assistance was sought if any or what action needed to be taken following the incident, such as referrals to other health professionals.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. The provider failed to ensure that medicines were managed safely. We reviewed medication administration records (MAR) that were inaccurate and contained information that was false. The provider told us that a senior staff member would video call staff and whilst they administer medicines, the staff would then sign the medicine record with the senior staff members name, even though they were not present when they administered the medicines. The provider told us this was because staff were not competent to administer medicines. Signing for someone else creates a false record of who administered the medication.This makes it difficult to track medication errors, identify patterns of missed doses, or trace the source of any adverse reactions. The provider had also failed to ensure the guidance was in place for ‘as required’ medicines. People who were prescribed ‘as required’ medicines for distress and anxiety did not have robust guidance in place. One person’s care plan detailed staff should ‘pre-emptively administer’ a sedative medicine. The medicines had been administered on 6 occasions in June 2025 and staff had not clearly detailed why the medicines was administered. We could not be assured that staff were administering the medicine appropriately, safely or in line with STOMP guidance. STOMP stands for stopping over medication of people with a learning disability, autism or both with psychotropic medicines.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not make sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They did not always make sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. They did not work together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. The provider failed to ensure staff were recruited safely. We reviewed staff files which had missing information, such as gaps in employment history and interview questions. The provider failed to ensure they completed checks on agency staff, this included making sure they had the relevant training. The provider failed to make sure all staff had completed the training they needed to support people safely. We identified 2 staff were on the rotas but were not on the training matrix. The provider could not evidence that these staff had completed training prior to supporting people and therefore we could not be assured that had the skills and competence to support people safely.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always detect and control potential risks in the care environment. The provider failed to ensure risks relating to the environment were effective. Information in people’s care plans around environmental risks were generic and not person specific. Care plans detailed for the person to ‘live in a safe well-maintained environment’ but no other information was detailed on how staff can support people to achieve this. We were not assured that people were being supported to maintain a safe environment.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people and health system partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. They did not manage or monitor people’s safety. The provider told us the majority of the staff team were agency staff. The provider told us they felt this gave a better of continuity of staff, however we found this not to be the case. We found that not all people had continuity of care from regular staff members. This consistency helps people feel secure, reduces anxiety, and allows them to develop stronger relationships with staff, ultimately improving their overall well-being and quality of life. People’s care and support was not coordinated, and the provider had not ensured that risks relating to people’s care journeys had been considered, for example, ensuring suitable training is in place for staff prior to staff supporting people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not work well with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and how to achieve that. They did not concentrate on improving people’s lives or protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider did not share concerns quickly and appropriately. The provider told us they did not have a safeguarding log as there had not been any safeguarding concerns; however, we found this was not the case. The provider had failed to ensure people were not subjected to unlawful physical restraint. The provider told us no one needed any physical interventions, however when we spoke to staff they described how they ‘held’ people and ‘hugged’ if they were distressed and would not let go if the person told them to. Unlawful restraint that is unnecessary or disproportionate is a form of physical abuse and may be considered a safeguarding concern. The provider had not ensured that people who were at risk of self-neglect had measures in place to safeguard them. One person’s daily notes identified they often refused their personal care; however, the provider did not have guidance in place to inform staff on how to support this person if they were neglecting themselves.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

This is the first assessment for this service at the new registered address. This key question has been rated inadequate.

This meant there were widespread and significant shortfalls in leadership. Leaders and the culture they created did not assure the delivery of high-quality care.

The service was in breach of legal regulation in relation to good governance.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support, or who embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. The provider had not ensured that high-quality leadership was sustained through safe, effective and inclusive recruitment and succession planning. The majority of staff were from other agencies and the staff recruited by the provider had not been done so in line with schedule 3 (this outlines specific information that must be held by providers of regulated activities concerning individuals employed or appointed to provide care). The provider had not considered succession for staff or continuity for people.

Leaders were not always alert to examples of poor culture or when it was identified this was not addressed quickly. The provider failed to ensure they had process in place to identify training needs. For example, some staff had a poor understanding of epilepsy and positive behaviour support, and this had not been identified prior to the inspection.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had not ensured that staff and leaders acted with openness, honesty and transparency. There was not a culture of speaking up and staff had not always raised concerns in relation to people’s care and support. For example, staff had not reported that they used physical interventions to support people and these interventions were not planned in the persons care plan.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They did not act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate. The provider was also the registered manager of the service. When we asked questions regarding the service and the people they supported they could not give us detailed answers. the registered manager did not understand their roles and responsibilities as a provider and registered manager.

The provider failed to ensure effective governance systems were in place across all aspects of the service. The provider failed to ensure effective audits were carried out to identify the risks that we found during the assessment.

The provider failed to ensure health risks were well managed and care plans contained the guidance needed for them to support people safely. The provider failed to ensure relevant or mandatory quality frameworks and recognised standards were considered and implemented. For example, the provider had not effectively incorporated best practice guidance, such as The REACH standards. The REACH standards are a set of 9 standards to ensure people with a learning disability and/or autistic people are supported to live how they choose, with the same rights as other citizens.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not focus on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They did not encourage creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They did not actively contribute to safe, effective practice and research.

The provider failed to research and implement recognised guidance to people. The provider had not followed the principles of Right support, right care, right culture (RSRCRC). The RSRCRC outlines that we expect health and social care providers to guarantee autistic people and people with a learning disability the choices, dignity, independence and good access to local communities that most people take for granted. For example, care plans did not detail or document clearly people’s choices around their care and support or their capacity to make choices.

The provider had not learnt from incidents. For example, one person had an incident where the required hospital treatment, their care and support plan were not updated to reflect this, and an assessment was not implemented to mitigate future risk.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider did not always understand their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They did not always share information and learning with partners or collaborate for improvement. The provider did not make sure there was continuity of care, the provider told us the majority of the staff team were made up of agency staff. People’s care and support was not always coordinated, and the provider had not ensured that risks relating to people’s care journeys had been considered.

However, some people’s care was coordinated, and they were supported by a number of different health professionals.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
There was a closed culture at the service. A "closed culture" is a poor culture that can lead to harm, including human rights breaches and abuse. We found a poor culture across the entire service, which had not been recognised or addressed by the provider. The provider did not have a shared vision, strategy and culture based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, and engagement. They did not understand the challenges and the needs of people and their communities. The provider had failed to be transparent with information that was requested from inspectors throughout the assessment, particularly around recruitment. The provider did not set a positive example to other staff in the organisation around transparency.

Effective systems were not in place to review the care people received, for example people’s care plans were very basic and lacked important information.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not value diversity in their workforce. The provider did not always take action to continually review and improve the culture of the organisation. The provider had not ensured staff were given a full induction and training prior to starting their role. For example, we identified staff who were detailed on the rota but not on the training matrix. We could not be assured that staff had been given the training they needed to support people safely but also ensure their rights as workers were met.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 1 - Evidence shows significant shortfalls in the standard of care
