asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Azure Care
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
Date of Assessment: 15 September to 20 October 2025. Azure Care Ltd is a domiciliary care agency providing personal care to people living in their own homes, including those with complex health needs, learning disabilities, autism, dementia, and physical disabilities. At the time of inspection 45people were receiving care and support from the agency. Not everyone who used the service received personal care. CQC only inspects where people receive personal care. This is help with tasks related to personal hygiene and eating.

A registered manager was in place. The registered managerwasregistered with the Commissionandwaslegally responsibleforensuringthe servicewascompliant with legal and regulatory requirements.

People received outstanding, person-centred care that was tailored to their individual preferences, routines, and cultural values. Staff demonstrated compassion, attentiveness, and professionalism, consistently promoting dignity, independence, and emotional wellbeing. The service was proactive in identifying risks and responding swiftly to concerns, including safeguarding alerts, nutritional needs, and environmental safety. For example, timely referrals to occupational therapy and fire safety services led to measurable improvements in people’s safety and quality of life.

Care plans were detailed and regularly reviewed, reflecting people’s evolving needs and preferences. Staff were well-trained, with access to specialist dementia training and resources to support meaningful engagement. The service demonstrated a strong learning culture, using audits, supervision, and feedback to drive continuous improvement. Innovative practices, such as the development of an AI-based care monitoring app, further exemplified the provider’s commitment to excellence.

The service met the principles of “Right support, right care, right culture” through its inclusive, respectful, and empowering approach to supporting people with learning disabilities and autistic people. Communication plans were highly personalised, enabling non-verbal individuals to participate fully in their care.

Complaints were minimal and handled effectively, with clear evidence of lessons learned. Compliments from people using the service, relatives, and professionals were frequent and heartfelt, describing Azure Care as “a silver lining” and “superstars.”

The provider was a finalist in multiple categories at the National Care Awards and the Great British Care Awards, reflecting sector-wide recognition of its outstanding service.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing exceptionally well.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience:
People told us and relatives confirmed that they felt safe and well supported by staff at Azure Care. Many described staff as reliable, respectful, and attentive to their needs. People consistently reported that staff arrived on time, wore appropriate protective equipment, and provided care in a way that made them feel secure. Several people highlighted the continuity of care and the benefit of having regular carers who understood their preferences and routines.

People said they were involved in their care planning and reviews, with a member of the management team conducting regular assessments and making adjustments where needed. Relatives confirmed that care plans were personalised and responsive to changing needs. People who managed their own medications felt supported, while others appreciated staff’s attentiveness in prompting or administering medicines safely.

Staff were described as caring and respectful, with many going “above and beyond” to support people’s wellbeing. People valued the rapport they had built with carers and noted that staff were discreet and sensitive when providing personal care. Several people shared examples of staff encouraging independence, such as supporting them to walk short distances or prepare meals.

Communication was praised, with people reporting that staff listened to concerns and responded promptly. Some people received newsletters and surveys, and others confirmed that their relatives were kept informed.

Relatives and people using the service spoke positively about the leadership, describing the manager and office staff as approachable and responsive. People appreciated the flexibility of the service, especially in emergencies or when additional support was needed. The service was described as well organised, with carers and office staff working together to ensure continuity and quality of care.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the service involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to outstanding. This meant people were truly respected and valued as individuals; and empowered as partners in their care in an exceptional service.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff worked proactively to empower people to have choice and control over their life whilst promoting their independence. Staff used visual tools and gestures to support non-verbal communication, enabling people to express preferences and maintain control over their care. People were given choices about meals, clothing, and routines, and staff adapted their approach to suit individual needs. This approach empowered the person to retain autonomy and dignity, with care delivered in a way that respected their capabilities and preferences.

Staff actively promoted people’s independence and supported choice. A person said, “They used to wash me in the morning till I was ready to do it myself. I take my time.” Another shared, “They always ask what I have eaten. They’d say, ‘Shall I make you a sandwich?’”

Another person wished to raise money for charity, a cause close to their heart by hosting a coffee morning. A member of the management team supported the person to plan and organise the event and then endured the staff team supporting the person were also not working and available to attend. The person sent a card to the team thanking them for their support to ensure the event took place and that it was a success.

Care plans detailed what people could do independently and how staff should support them. For example, a person was supported to wash their top half independently, with staff providing tools like a toothbrush with toothpaste already applied to enable them to complete this task independently.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff consistently demonstrated kindness and compassion in their interactions with people. A person said, “They [staff] are very friendly and helpful to my needs. I have no worries about staff showering me. They are quite discrete.” Another person shared, “They always come. They’re nice, like bringing the milk and bread in, changing the beds. We didn’t ask.”

During a joint visit with Medway Community Healthcare’s Urgent Response Team, an occupational therapist observed a carer supporting a person with mobility needs and described their approach as “compassionate, attentive and professional.”

The provider maintained a compliments log, with relatives expressing gratitude for the “loving environment” created during end-of-life care. A family wrote, “Everyone at Azure… made [Name] as happy as they could be in their final days.”

These examples show that staff not only delivered care with empathy but also created meaningful relationships that had a lasting impact on people’s wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff responded promptly and effectively to people’s changing needs. During a care call a member of staff noticed a wound on a persons’ leg and immediately contacted emergency services, staying until the ambulance arrived. The family later wrote to praise the carer’s swift action, saying it likely prevented sepsis.

Another person shared, “They organised a district nurse” after noticing a skin issue which they [staff] were concerned about.

Staff were trained to recognise signs of distress and escalate concerns, including safeguarding alerts and referrals to external professionals. During a care call of a person that lived alone staff noticed they were in a low mood and showing signs of emotional distress. Staff acted immediately contacting the local authority and the persons’ relative. Staff concerned about the persons ‘well-being so they stayed with the person until their relative arrived. Additional welfare and social support visits were implemented which increased the persons’ mood and well-being. The person later gave the agency a five-star [five being the highest] review writing, “Following being let down by my previous care provider, I can honestly say Azure Care has been a silver lining. I feel truly blessed that circumstances have given me such a valued opportunity to be a client of Azure Care. The professionalism and compassion shown by the team have been second to none.”

Daily notes showed that staff adapted care based on people’s presentation and consent was consistently sought. For example, when a person’s appetite declined, carers introduced lunch visits and monitored hydration, resulting in improved fluid intake and weight stability.

These examples show that staff were proactive and responsive, with actions leading to measurable improvements in people’s health and wellbeing.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were treated as individuals, with care tailored to their preferences, routines, and beliefs. A person said, “They know what soaps and shampoos to use. They moisturise her.” Another shared, “They follow the shopping list and photograph it on their phone.”

People with communication challenges were supported through personalised strategies. A person who did not use verbal communication had a communication plan that included gesture recognition and emotional cues. This enabled the person to make daily choices and feel safe and included in their care.

Staff supported another person to attend a family holiday which they hadn’t been able to participate in for a number of years. Staff offered the person bespoke care and support for the journey and during the holiday to ensure their personal aspirations and goals were met and exceeded.

People’s identities were respected and their preferences upheld, resulting in improved emotional wellbeing and trust in the service. For example, people’s care plans included detailed personal histories, religious and cultural needs. For example, one persons’ request for a 6:00 a.m. visit to accommodate their morning prayers was respected and implemented, with culturally matched care staff assigned.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff felt valued, supported, and proud of their roles. The provider promoted a positive culture through biannual team meetings, weekly emails, and open-door policies. Staff described management as “always available,” “very caring,” and “supportive with childcare and personal needs”. Staff were recognised through awards and praised for their contributions to the service’s nomination in national care awards. Training was comprehensive, including dementia simulation experiences and regular supervision. A carer said, “This training changed how I think and how I support people living with dementia”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has changed to outstanding. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently better than expected compared to similar services. People’s feedback described it as exceptional and distinctive.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. Initial assessments were thorough and person-centred, capturing medical history, preferences, and social context. A person said, “2 people came out and interviewed me, and saw what all my needs were.” Care plans were regularly reviewed, and people confirmed they were involved in these reviews.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff consistently sought consent before providing care. People confirmed that carers asked permission before entering their homes or assisting with personal care. A person said, “Staff always ask permission. I have a key safe, and the girls and the office staff have the number.” Staff had received training on the Mental Capacity Act and understood how to apply it in practice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: Care and support were delivered in line with best practice. Staff followed detailed care plans and used clinical guidance to support nutrition, hydration, and skin integrity. For example, a person with weight loss received additional lunch visits, resulting in improved food intake and hydration. Staff were trained in dementia care and used tailored approaches, such as the virtual dementia tour, to enhance empathy and effectiveness.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff worked together effectively to deliver joined-up care and support. People benefitted from strong communication between carers, office staff, and external professionals. A person told us, “Staff always come at the same time and know exactly what I need. They talk to each other and keep me in the loop.”

Staff adapted their approach for people with communication challenges. For example, a person, who did not use verbal communication, had a personalised communication plan that included gesture interpretation, picture books, and emotional cues. Carers were trained to recognise signs of discomfort and offer meaningful choices. This helped the person feel safe and included in their care.

When a person expressed suicidal thoughts, staff escalated concerns immediately and coordinated with the local authorities’ safeguarding team. A welfare visit was arranged, and the person was supported to join a local social club. This intervention improved their mental health and reduced isolation.

Staff described open communication with district nurses, occupational therapists, and GPs. A carer said, “We call the district nurse if we see any skin changes. They always respond quickly, and we work together to keep the person safe.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider monitored outcomes effectively and used data to improve care. Care records showed clear evidence of impact, such as increased hydration and improved emotional wellbeing following targeted interventions. A person said, “They noticed I wasn’t eating properly and changed my care. Now I feel stronger and more like myself.”

Staff understood people’s expectations of their care and ensured these were met and exceeded. People’s health, independence and mobility had all improved with support from staff.

Incident logs were analysed to identify patterns and learning. For example, after a fall, the care team reviewed the person’s environment and made a referral to occupational therapy. This led to changes in equipment and reduced future risk.

People’s feedback was used to improve service delivery. A person said, “They changed my lunchtime call so I could eat properly. It’s made a big difference.”

Staff used digital tools to track progress and identify trends. The service was developing an AI-based app to analyse visit data in real time, helping to flag emerging risks and improve continuity of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to live healthier lives through proactive care planning and health promotion. Staff monitored nutrition and hydration closely and acted early to prevent deterioration. For example, a person’s care package was adapted to include a lunch visit after staff noticed reduced food intake. Their fluid intake nearly doubled over three months, and their weight stabilised following these additional visits. People told us staff encouraged them to eat well and stay active. A person said, “They [staff] always ask what I’ve had to eat and make sure I drink enough. I feel better now.”

A person expressed a wish to attend their own health appointments within the local community however; they did not have the required wheelchair to enable this. With the persons’ consent care staff advocated on the persons’ behalf and liaised with the local authority and the correct professionals to ensure the person received the appropriate equipment to enable their social and medical connection whilst increasing their independence.

Staff were trained in pressure ulcer prevention and worked with tissue viability teams to support people with complex skin care needs. This reduced the risk of hospital admission and improved outcomes.

Staff used seasonal health tips and provided personal safety equipment, such as visibility strips and alarms, to promote wellbeing. Staff also supported people to attend medical appointments and access community services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the service met people’s needs.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff understood people’s needs and provided consistent care. Continuity was supported through the electronic rostering system, which prioritised regular carers based on client preferences, such as language, gender, and communication style.

Transitions between services were well-managed. The provider demonstrated effective discharge planning, including hospital visits to reassess needs and update care plans before people returned home.

Relatives confirmed that staff were responsive to changes. A family member said, “The office adjusted the rota so [Name] could continue their morning prayers. It meant so much to [Name].”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service ensured equitable access to care. Staff were matched to clients based on language and cultural preferences, and adjustments were made to accommodate religious practices, such as early morning visits for prayer.

Referrals were made to external services when risks were identified, including fire safety assessments and occupational therapy support.

Staff were trained in equality and diversity, and recruitment practices promoted inclusivity.

The management team took part in an on-call system to ensure a member of the management team was available for advice or support at anytime for people using the service or staff.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider promoted a culture of openness and inclusion. People’s experiences were celebrated through cultural events and personalised care. For example, staff brought Easter eggs and Christmas biscuits to clients, fostering a sense of belonging.

Outcomes were monitored and improved through proactive interventions. A person’s hydration and nutrition improved significantly following the introduction of a lunch visit, with fluid intake nearly doubling over three months.

Feedback from relatives highlighted the impact of care. A family wrote, “Azure Care made [Name]’s last chapter at home so rich and rewarding,” praising the team’s compassion and responsiveness.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider listened to people and acted on their feedback. Adjustments were made to care routines based on individual preferences, such as changing visit times or adapting food preparation methods.

Concerns were addressed promptly. For example, when a person felt a carer was disinterested, the field care supervisor conducted a spot check and followed up with supervision to ensure improvements.

People felt heard and respected. A person shared, “They’re quick, [carer] but they’re patient with me when I’m getting dressed. I have a routine.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with people, how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. Care plans were highly personalised and included detailed instructions tailored to individual preferences, such as preferred flannels, food choices, and routines. For example, a person’s care plan specified the exact temperature of water used during personal care and the preferred strength of squash, which was respected and reinforced through staff training and supervision.

People consistently described staff as respectful, kind, and responsive. A person said, “They always ask me what I want to wear and help me when I need it,” while another shared, “They treat me with dignity and give me privacy.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Future planning was embedded in care delivery. Digital care plans included sections on capacity, DNACPR, Advance Decisions, and end-of-life preferences. These were updated in real time and accessible to staff.

End-of-life care was delivered with compassion and dignity. Families described the support as “loving” and “amazing,” with carers becoming “an extension of the family.”

Although no clients were receiving end-of-life care at the time of inspection, the provider had robust protocols in place, ready to activate when needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People received information in ways that suited them. Care plans included communication preferences, and staff used clear, respectful language. For example, a person’s niece was kept informed of all care updates due to her Power of Attorney status.

Weekly rotas were emailed to people, and newsletters were sent regularly. Staff also used the electronic app to record care notes, which were accessible to next of kin.

Feedback mechanisms were in place, including surveys and courtesy calls. One person said, “They always ask how I’m doing and if anything needs changing.”

The agency was meeting the principles of the Accessible information standard. All documents were available in formats to meet peoples’ needs such as, larger print and pictorial.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff used personal protective equipment (PPE) appropriately and followed infection control procedures. Training was completed annually, and staff described using gloves, aprons, and masks consistently. People confirmed, “They [staff] wear PPE: a mask, an apron and gloves, and their Identity badge”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were actively involved in managing risks related to their care. Risk assessments were detailed and person-centred, with mitigation actions clearly recorded. For example, following a fall, the provider reviewed care records with the person and their spouse, and made a referral to occupational therapy. Each risk was scored and control measures were implemented, such as equipment checks and skin integrity monitoring.

A person said, “The co-ordinator came round and did risk assessments. [Name] does the care plan reviews. She is so approachable.”

This proactive approach enabled people to remain safe while maintaining independence and choice.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. Staff discussed incidents in team meetings and made changes to care plans to reduce risks. For example, following a fall, the care team reviewed responsibilities and updated the care plan to include bin management during visits.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary: People received medicines safely, with clear care records and regular audits. Staff had been trained and followed the 7 Rs of medication administration right patient, right medication, right dose, right route, right time, right reason, right documentation and used electronic MARs to record topical medication. A person said, “Staff sort my medication. They give me a little blue cup and give me my medicines”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary: People received care from a consistent staff team who were well-trained and recruited safely. Staff felt supported and received regular support and supervision. The electronic rostering system prioritised regular carers, and staff described feeling valued and respected. A person said, “They [staff] are always on time. They take me to hospital appointments and give me support”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: People lived in safe environments that were regularly assessed for risks. Environmental assessments included fire safety, utilities, and room-specific hazards. Where fire safety concerns were identified the agency took a proactive approach, referrals were made to Kent Fire and Rescue Service who visited the person in their home and took action. For example, a person who was hard of hearing and living with dementia received a visual and vibrating alarm system beside their bed, ensuring they could be alerted in case of fire. Another couple received tailored evacuation advice and had their smoke alarm relocated for better effectiveness. Other people who were at identified risk and lived alone received targeted fire and practical safety advice. Batteries in smoke alarms were replaced for some people. These actions significantly improved the safety of people within their homes in the event of an emergency. These adaptations had a measurable impact on people’s safety and peace of mind, particularly for those at higher risk due to health or environmental factors. Families reported feeling reassured and confident in the safety of their loved ones.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider ensured people experienced safe and well-coordinated transitions between services. Staff advocated for people during hospital admissions and proactively planned for discharge. For example, when a person was admitted to hospital, carers attended to share the persons’ care preferences with medical staff. Prior to discharge from hospital, staff visited the person to assess any changes in need, and supervisors attended initial home visits to adjust care arrangements. [JB1][KW2]A person said, “They came to hospital to discuss, and then back at home with proposals.” This approach ensured continuity of care and reduced the risk of readmission. People felt reassured and supported during vulnerable transitions.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff were trained in safeguarding and followed the provider’s policy. Safeguarding was a standard agenda item for meetings. Staff described safeguarding as “protecting clients from harm, abuse or neglect” and knew how to escalate concerns. A person said, “They [staff] are very professional in how they deal with me. You can talk to them about anything”.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this assessment the rating has remained good. This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary: The registered manager demonstrated the skills and experience to lead the service effectively. Staff described the manager as approachable and responsive. A staff member said, “He is very caring and approachable and shows concern for me.” People using the service and their relatives confirmed the manager was visible and involved, with 1 person stating, “[The registered manager] has been out to see me. He is a nice man. He did a courtesy visit when I came out of hospital.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff felt confident to raise concerns and were aware of the whistleblowing policy. They described a culture of openness and said they were listened to. A staff member told us, “If we have any concern then we can let the office know and they will listen and advise us.” The provider had systems in place to record and respond to complaints, with evidence of lessons learned and actions taken.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary: Governance systems were in place to monitor quality and safety. Audits were completed regularly, and actions were taken in response to findings. The provider had a service development plan that identified areas for improvement and tracked progress.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service demonstrated a strong culture of continuous learning and innovation. Staff were encouraged to reflect on incidents and share lessons learned. A central log of incidents and accidents was maintained, with analysis used to identify patterns and drive improvements. For example, following a fall, a referral was made to occupational therapy, and care plans were updated to reduce future risk.

The provider had begun developing an AI-powered care application to analyse client visit data in real time, aiming to identify emerging risks and improve continuity of care. This proactive approach to technology demonstrated a forward-thinking attitude to service improvement.

Staff attended specialist training such as the virtual dementia tour, which simulated symptoms of dementia to deepen empathy and understanding. Feedback from staff included, “It changed my way of thinking and the way I support people living with dementia,” showing the impact of training on practice.

The organisation was recognised externally, being finalists in both the National Care Awards and the South East Region Great British Care Awards. Staff were praised for their contribution, with the registered manager stating, “We couldn’t have done this without you – thank you for everything you do!”.

Weekly emails were used to share updates, policy reminders, and examples of positive outcomes, embedding a culture of learning and celebration. Staff meetings were held biannually and supplemented with ad hoc sessions to ensure all staff received consistent information and had opportunities to contribute.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 4 - Evidence shows an exceptional standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The service worked in partnership with external professionals and community organisations. Staff described positive relationships with district nurses, occupational therapists, and safeguarding teams. Referrals were made to the Kent Fire and Rescue Service when risks were identified, resulting in improved safety outcomes for people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The management team promoted a positive and open culture that was shared with the staff team. Staff described the organisation as supportive and inclusive, with regular communication through biannual meetings and weekly emails. These emails included updates, policy reminders, and recognition of staff achievements, such as being finalists in national care awards. Staff told us, “They always congratulate us and say well done for your hard work which makes us feel appreciated.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The leadership team actively promoted a culture of inclusion and respect, ensuring that staff felt valued and supported regardless of background. Staff consistently described the organisation as inclusive and responsive to their individual needs. A staff member shared, “I have allergies to pets and they have listened to me and allocated me clients who have no pets,” demonstrating reasonable adjustments made during allocation.

Staff were encouraged to disclose any health or personal circumstances during recruitment, and adjustments were made accordingly. For example, a carer recovering from surgery was assigned non-manual handling tasks to support their recovery.

The organisation celebrated cultural diversity through events such as Eid, Diwali, and Christmas, and ensured that people using the service were matched with carers who understood their cultural and linguistic preferences. A person’s care was adapted to begin at 6:00 a.m. to support their spiritual practice of morning prayers, with carers selected who shared an understanding of their faith.

Equality and diversity training was mandatory and refreshed annually. Staff demonstrated understanding of protected characteristics and described how they respected religious and cultural preferences in daily care routines. The provider’s commitment to equity was evident in both policy and practice, and no concerns were raised regarding discrimination.

asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Cathrolls' UK Limited
asgRatings.name: Homecare
asgRatings.commentary:
We carried out this comprehensive assessment between 15 April 2025 and 02 May 2025. This was the first assessment/inspection of the service since it registered with CQC. We looked at how Cathrolls’ UK Limited assessed people's care needs, and how they trained and supervised staff to support people according to their needs and preferences. Cathrolls’ UK Limited is a domiciliary care service providing personal care to people in their own homes in the community. At the time of our inspection there were 2 people using the service who required support with their personal care. Not everyone who used the service received personal care. CQC only inspects where people receive personal care. This is help with tasks related to personal hygiene and eating. Where they do we also consider any wider social care provided. The service provides support to older people, people living with dementia, people with physical disabilities and people with a sensory impairment. We spoke with 2 people, 1 relative and 4 staff including the registered manager and nominated individual during the assessment. The nominated individual is responsible for supervising the management of the service on behalf of the provider.

People were protected from avoidable harm because risk assessments were in place however, these were not always clear, comprehensive and up to date. The management team updated these during the assessment to ensure staff had updated information about providing safe care and support. Staff were not always recruited safely as the provider had not explored their full employment history. However, the provider had carried out relevant checks and gained references before staff started as well as carrying out home office right to work in the UK checks which mitigated the risk. The provider had systems and processes in place to understand the diverse health and care needs of people receiving a service. Systems and processes to audit and check the service were in place, however these were not always robust. We identified shortfalls in record keeping which had the potential to cause impact as the service expands. We discussed these with the provider who agreed that improvements were required. They amended some records during the assessment. Staff felt communication was effective. Staff were supported through training; some additional training was required to ensure staff had all the training they needed. Staff had been adequately deployed at times that met people’s needs, they had sufficient travel time between people they supported. People and relatives were treated with respect and kindness.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: People's feedback about the service they received was positive. Comments included, “I am fortunate to have them” and “They are definitely respectful of my privacy and dignity.” People's relatives told us their loved ones were safe and well looked after. They were kept informed about changes in health or incidents and accidents. A relative said, “We have had Cathrolls for 5-6 years now. He’s safe and being well looked after. The quality of care has been brilliant.”

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good. This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider promoted people’s independence, so people knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and wellbeing. People lived independently in their own homes. Some people lived with relatives. They were supported to do things that were important to them such as going shopping or medical appointment by their relatives. People told us staff make time to chat with them as part of their care and support which they valued. A staff member told us, “[Person] is aware of everything, he loves to chat and ask questions.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider always treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Staff treated colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect. People and their relatives told us that they were treated with respect and kindness. People said, “They are kind and courteous” and “They are friendly. They knock the door before they come in.” A relative told us, “Dad’s care is fantastic, he near enough has 1:1, he loves [staff member] to bits. The carers really care. They have a good rapport.” Staff detailed how they treated people with kindness and compassion. A staff member said, “I make sure the door is locked when supporting in the shower, help to get dressed before moving back to the bedroom. It is important to protect dignity and carry out personal care in private. I close curtains and only open them when the person is fully dressed.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider listened to and understood people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff responded to people’s needs in the moment and acted to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress. Relatives felt staff knew their loved one well and felt their loved one was happy and safe. A relative said, “They are on the end of the phone if I need to make contact. [Nominated individual] is fine. I have no issues getting in contact with the office.” The management team explained thar sometimes staff supported with additional tasks to support people. For example, food shopping and ordering medicines.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics. People’s care plans which had been reviewed and amended following our assessment site visit showed what people could do for themselves, for example washing their own chest or cleaning their own teeth once toothpaste had been applied to the brush. Staff knew people well. A relative told us, “He’s being looked after well. I am happy.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider cared about and promoted the wellbeing of their staff, and supported and enabled staff to always deliver person-centred care. There was a diverse workforce where staff were treated as individuals. A member of staff said, “They made me very comfortable when I came and made it easier. Thumbs up for them.” Staff were supported through supervision meetings, appraisals and training. The management team told us they had altered a member of staff’s shift times during a religious festival they observed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them. The provider carried out assessments of people’s needs prior to their package of care and support starting. The assessments were then reviewed monthly. Staff told us they reported any changes to people’s care and support needs to the management team. A staff member said, “If anything changes, I call management. If I notice anything I let them know.” A relative told us “They are on the ball (with noticing issues/changes).”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) provides a legal framework for making particular decisions on behalf of people who may lack the mental capacity to do so for themselves. The MCA requires that, as far as possible, people make their own decisions and are helped to do so when needed. When they lack mental capacity to take particular decisions, any made on their behalf must be in their best interests and as least restrictive as possible. We checked whether the service was working within the principles of the MCA.

People told us they made choices and day to day decisions about their lives. A person told us, “They talk with me and guide me.” People’s care records evidenced that staff respected people’s choices and decisions. A staff member said, “Everyone we support has capacity and can make their own choices.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards. People were provided with care and support which met their needs and expectations. A person told us, “My priority is a shower and dress up and they support me with that and to comb my hair.” When people had support with preparing and cooking food, the food provided was purchased by relatives and cooked by staff. People were making food choices.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services. The provider told us that they shared information about health concerns with relevant healthcare professionals and with relatives. They had also provided advice to people using the service and their families when they noticed areas of concern outside of their commissioned role. For example, providing advice about footcare to people. A person told us, “If I need anything extra, I ask, and they do it for me.” The staff team was small and worked well together. The nominated individual for the provider also provided care and support when required and knew people well. A member of staff told us, “I feel well supported, we work as a team, we get information about changes.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves. The provider carried out monthly telephone monitoring reviews of the service to check that people were happy with their care. We could see that adjustments had been made to care and support in relation to the feedback. There had been no complaints about the service. Compliments about the service were not recorded. People told us, “I have no problems with them” and “I have not really got any complaints. They are pretty good.”

Supervisions and spot checks had taken place frequently, staff were provided with an opportunity to discuss any concerns they may have about people’s care or how it could be improved. A member of staff told us, “I have regular spot checks and supervision. I may have 2 to 3 spot checks per month.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider supported people to manage their health and wellbeing to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support. Staff could tell us how they would access additional support from healthcare professionals to help people manage their health, should they be required. The management team gave us examples of when they had made contact with people’s GP or the district nursing service when people had suffered a reaction to prescribed medicines and when there had been problems with a person’s stoma. Records showed that staff had received training to support people with their specific health or lifelong conditions, such as stoma care and dementia. Records showed staff had not undertaken training in diabetes and oxygen therapy even though they supported people who had diabetes and who used oxygen. The management team advised they would address this. A relative told us, “If there is anything health wise they get it touch, they are brilliant."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good. This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider understood the diverse health and care needs of people and their local communities, so care was joined-up, flexible and supported choice and continuity. The service worked with other health professionals involved in people’s care. Information was shared with staff regarding any changes to people’s health or care needs. Staff told us how they supported people and their relatives. A staff member said, “When an NHS letter comes for [person] I help him open it, pin it on the fridge and let his son know, his son is very involved and provides support to go to the appointment.” Relatives told us they felt staff communicated well them well.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it. People lived independently in their own homes in the community and managed their own daily activities and community engagement. We had difficulty getting in contact with the service and the management team before the assessment and during the assessment because the phone lines were not accepting calls. Despite this, people and their relatives told us they were always able to make contact with the service when they needed to. The management team told us that sometimes staff supported people with additional tasks to meet their needs such as essential food shopping or liaising with the pharmacy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary: Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this. People had opportunities to feedback to the management team about their service. The nominated individual for the provider visited people regularly which enabled people to discuss their needs and expectations. A person told us, “[Nominated individual] comes every 6 months, [Nominated individual] keeps in touch to see if there are any concerns and she visits. I can always get hold of [Nominated individual].” It was clear from the care records that people had time to chat with staff as part of their care visits. This showed that visits were not task focused. People also had support from their relatives and loved ones.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result. The provider carried out monthly telephone monitoring calls and regular visits to people using the service. Relatives told us that the service was responsive to their loved ones needs. Staff described how they listened and respected people.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with people, how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs. People told us their care and support was person centred, they had consistent staff that knew them well. Staff described how they supported people at their own pace. A staff member said, “When providing personal care for [person], we make sure his clothes are ready, he needs a lot of time and we don’t rush."

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary: People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life. Some people had a DNACPR (Do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation) form in place. This is an advanced decision not to attempt CPR. It is not about other treatments or care. Staff told us they had received training to support them to provide end of life care when needed. At the time of the assessment, no one was at the end of their life.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs. People were able to access information. Although not required at the time of the inspection, the service had pictorial communication aids if needed and also access to translation services should they need it. Staff were aware of people’s individual communication needs for example, people who may have hearing or vision impairments.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good. This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly. The provider had an up to date infection prevention and control (IPC) policy. Staff had completed IPC training. Staff told us they had access to personal protective equipment (PPE) to keep themselves and people safe. A staff member said, “I have gloves, masks and aprons. I call when I am running low and collect these from the office.” The provider carried out spot checks of staff practice which included checks to make sure staff were using PPE appropriately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always work well with people to understand and manage risks. Staff did not always provide care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them. The provider had not always considered risks relating to providing care and support and had not detailed clear actions for staff to mitigate risks. For example, risks of infection relating to contact with bodily fluids and cross infection from healthcare related infections, which put them at risk of harm. After the site visit the registered manager amended the risk assessments and care plans to provide clearer guidance for staff. Staff told us they have access to risk assessments and care plans. A staff member said, “Care plans and risk assessments are on the app, it includes information about security details and medicines.” A person told us that staff were aware of risks relating to equipment in their home.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice. There had not been any accidents, incidents or events that had occurred at the service. The provider and registered manager told us that if any occurred they would investigate the issues, review practice and make any changes that are required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. The provider had medicines policies and procedures in place. The service was only providing medicines support to 1 person. Medicines administration records showed that the person had received their medicines as prescribed. However, where they were prescribed medicated patches to place on their skin, for example, to control symptoms, they were not administered following prescriber's guidance. Patches can cause irritation to the skin if they are placed in the same position after removal. There was a risk people, who may already have frail skin, could experience a reaction and discomfort. We found no evidence that people had been harmed. Staff had received medicines training. A staff member said, “I have had medicines training, we get spot checks all the time, without telling us.” A relative told us, “They support him with his medicines, I do the ordering.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff. They made sure staff received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs. Staff were not always recruited safely. Staff recruitment records showed gaps in staff employment history. These gaps had not been addressed and recorded. The provider’s application forms only asked applicants for 10 years of employment history and not their full employment history. This meant the provider was not able to demonstrate that they had a full employment history for each employee as required. The provider advised they would amend their application forms for future use. They amended their recruitment policy to reflect that a full employment history was required. The impact of this issue was low as staff had undergone checks by the home office prior to working for the service. Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) criminal record checks were completed as well as reference checks. DBS checks provide information including details about convictions and cautions held on the Police National Computer. The information helps employers make safer recruitment decisions.

Staff reported they had travel time allocated to them to enable them to travel between care visits. We observed that there were enough staff deployed to meet people’s planned care needs. A person told us, “I have care visits 7 days per week, they turn up on time and always stay the right amount of time.”

The provider’s training records showed staff had completed most training to meet people’s assessed needs. Training records did not show that staff had attended training in relation to oxygen. A person used oxygen in their home to maintain their health. The provider’s training policy stated that staff would be given mandatory training in learning disability and autism. They were not following this policy as staff had not completed the training. There was no impact on people they were supporting as the service was not providing care and support to people with a learning disability or autistic people. A staff member told us, “I love to learn so I indulge myself with online training. I have gained experience working for Cathrolls, the training has been superb. My next training is due in May. The training is a mix of training online and face to face, for example last year we redid hoisting training all over again and practiced this, there was a competency check.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care. Risks relating to the environments staff were working in had not been fully assessed. For example, risks relating to access, egress, flooring, lighting, location of emergency shut offs for gas, electric and water. We discussed this with the provider and registered manager. They advised they would review the risk assessments and add additional information to ensure staff had all the info they needed to keep themselves and people safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services. The provider carried out assessments of people’s needs prior to their package of care and support starting. This enabled them to meet people in their own homes. Staff told us care plans and risk assessments were in place when they carried out their care and support visits. A person told us, “They write it all down in a book before they leave, they do it when they have finished.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The provider shared concerns quickly and appropriately. People were safe and were protected from harm. Safeguarding and whistleblowing policies were in place and were accessible to staff. Staff were aware of the safeguarding policy. A member of staff said, “I have done safeguarding training. I would report abuse to the office, I can raise the alarm and speak with social services or the police if I need to. The manager would definitely deal with it.” People told us they felt safe.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. This is the first assessment for this newly registered service. This key question has been rated good. This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty. The management team knew people well and were passionate about making sure people received good quality care. Staff understood their responsibilities to meet regulatory requirements. The registered manager was supported by the nominated individual for the provider.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard. Complaints processes were available. A relative confirmed the management team were responsive and accessible. Staff confirmed they were invited to meetings and encouraged to contribute. Staff felt listened to. A staff member said, “I will give them a score of 85 to 90% for responsiveness, to be active and to respond on time.” Staff meeting minutes evidenced that these took place regularly. Staff told us they were encouraged to voice their ideas for improvements and any concerns. Staff knew how to raise concerns with the provider or outside organisations if they needed to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider did not always have clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability or good governance. They did not always act on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, or share this securely with others when appropriate. It was not clear that a robust system of audits and checks were in place to provide the registered manager and provider oversight. Records management required improvement, some records were missing or not completed. Records and filing appeared to be chaotic which was concerning when the service was only providing support to a few people. Audits and checks had been completed quarterly for the last 9 months but no other audits and checks had been completed prior to this. Some policies and procedures had different names of people and services listed in them and had not been reviewed to ensure they were relevant to domiciliary care. Audits and checks had not picked these issues up. The provider had not informed CQC of a change of telephone number for the service. Since the site visit a notification has now been received. Despite these issues, people were receiving good quality care and support and had not been impacted. Staff told us spot checks were taking place frequently.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research. The registered manager and nominated individual for the provider told us they had reviewed the feedback we gave them as part of the onsite and offsite assessment process and valued this. They were using the feedback to make improvements to the service and to put systems in place to embed the changes.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement. The management team were keen to build links with partnership agencies and had liaised with the local authority and local integrated care board. The registered manager was involved in forums and events to keep abreast of local and national developments in health and social care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities. The management team were passionate about the service and wanted to ensure people had good quality care and improved outcomes. The provider’s statement of purpose stated ‘Cathrolls’ UK Limited aim to assist those in need of care, to live as safely and comfortably as possible in their own homes. We will do this by actively encouraging the independence, dignity, privacy, choice and wellbeing of all our Service Users. Our principal belief is one of delivering a continual high quality service and developing relationships that actively encourage our Service Users own wellbeing.’ We found that the service was achieving their aims. The staff gave positive feedback about the culture of the service. Staff reported a positive open culture where they felt empowered to raise any concerns or make suggestions. A staff member said, “So far so good with support from managers.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary: The provider valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them. Staff felt they were treated well and supported equally by management. The provider had processes in place to encourage an inclusive culture, and support was in place for staff. Any issues could be discussed openly at staff meetings or during supervision. Staff told us they would not hesitate to speak to the management team if they needed to.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
