The provider had stepped back from day-to-day operations and had employed a new registered manager and new office staff, including supervisors and care co-ordinators. The service was also being over seen by a new operations manager who also is the Nominated individual. The nominated individual is responsible for supervising the management of the service on behalf of the provider.

At this inspection, we found that the service had made meaningful progress across most areas, particularly in culture, communication, training, care planning and staff supervision. People and families consistently told us they experienced kinder, more reliable care, and staff described clearer expectations under the new registered manager and nominated individual.

Despite this progress, improvements had not been yet fully embedded due to time. Governance systems—introduced only recently—had not consistently identified issues, and in some cases, inspectors identified concerns that internal audits had missed. This meant leaders could not yet fully assure themselves, at time of inspection, that care was safe and consistently managed.
Medicines management and risk assessment remained an area of concern. Although the registered manager had taken steps to improve practice, there were still gaps in MAR charts, incomplete audits and insufficiently detailed risk assessments. Some risks, such as the use of flammable creams, had not been appropriately assessed until raised during inspection. Once raised, these were remedied immediately.

Overall, the service is moving in the right direction, and many improvements have had a positive impact on people’s experiences. The registered manager and nominated individual had created a more open, supportive and responsive culture. Governance, medicines and risk management require further time to fully demonstrate appropriate oversight and consistency.
Feedback given to the registered manager and the nominated individual was accepted and acted upon immediately.

This service has been in Special Measures since 16 April 2025. The purpose of special measures is to ensure that services providing inadequate care make significant improvements. Special measures provide a framework within which we use our enforcement powers in response to inadequate care and provide a time frame within which providers must improve the quality of the care they provide.
The registered manager demonstrated improvements that have been made. The service is no longer rated as inadequate overall or in any of the key questions. Therefore, this service is no longer in Special Measures.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.
asgRatings.overallPeopleExperience: Feedback from people and their relatives was similar to the previous inspection. People and relatives, we spoke with stated they were happy with the service. Relatives told us staff were on time and calls were rarely missed. Relatives knew how to raise concerns with the office and found they had been responsive and told us there had been a service wide improvement in the last 6-12 months and since the new management team had been put in place. People were receiving a safer, more person centred and dignified service and feedback on the staff teams was generally positive.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Caring – this means we looked for evidence that the provider involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.
At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people were supported and treated with dignity and respect; and involved as partners in their care.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager promoted people’s independence, so people knew their rights and had choice and control over their own care, treatment and well being.

Staff promoted people’s independence and supported them to maintain as much control over their daily lives as possible. Care plans included guidance about what people could do for themselves and how staff should encourage and support independence safely.
People told us they were given choices throughout their care, such as what they wanted to wear, eat or do that day. A relative told us, “Yes, they do talk to them about what they are about to do. They never force my parents to do anything if they say no.” Staff explained options clearly and checked people’s preferences during each visit. This helped people understand their rights and remain in control of their care and well being.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager always treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity. Staff treated colleagues from other organisations with kindness and respect.

People told us staff treated them with kindness, empathy and compassion. They said staff took time to listen, speak respectfully and did not rush their visits. People described staff as “gentle,” “patient,” and “considerate,” and told us they felt comfortable and at ease during care. Staff also respected people’s privacy and dignity. They described how they ensured doors and curtains were closed during personal care, explained each step before providing support and sought permission before touching or assisting someone. Staff extended this respectful approach to colleagues from external organisations, ensuring collaborative working was courteous and professional.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager listened to and understood people’s needs, views and wishes. Staff responded to people’s needs in the moment and acted to minimise any discomfort, concern or distress.
Staff listened carefully and responded promptly to people’s needs, views and wishes. People said staff were attentive and adjusted their support when they noticed discomfort or changes in mood. Daily records showed staff took action to relieve distress or concern—such as offering reassurance, rearranging tasks to suit the person’s pace, or notifying family members or health professionals when appropriate.
Staff demonstrated an understanding of people’s emotional well being, supporting them sensitively during times of anxiety, illness or bereavement.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager treated people as individuals and made sure people’s care, support and treatment met people’s needs and preferences. They took account of people’s strengths, abilities, aspirations, culture and unique backgrounds and protected characteristics.

Staff treated people as individuals and tailored care to their needs and preferences. Care records demonstrated improved detail about people’s strengths, cultural backgrounds, religious practices, aspirations and personal routines. Staff recognised the importance of people’s protected characteristics and adapted their approach accordingly.

People and their relatives told us staff understood “what matters” to them—for example, the time they preferred their meals, how they wanted personal care delivered, or how they liked their home environment to be left. This approach supported people to feel valued and understood. We were told, “They are kind and considerate and listen to my mother’s wishes as well.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager cared about and promoted the well being of their staff and supported and enabled staff to always deliver person-centred care.
The registered manager and nominated individual demonstrated a commitment to staff well being and development. Staff told us they felt valued, supported and listened to, and that the management team were approachable and responsive. Regular supervision sessions encouraged staff to reflect on their practice and identify training needs, supporting them to deliver person-centred care. Staff described a positive shift in the culture of the service since the last inspection and since the new management team had been implemented, with improved communication, clearer expectations and better teamwork. This supported the consistent and compassionate care people experienced.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Effective – this means we looked for evidence that people’s care, treatment and support achieved good outcomes and promoted a good quality of life, based on best available evidence.
At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people’s outcomes were consistently good, and people’s feedback confirmed this.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.
People’s needs had been reassessed following the last inspection to ensure care delivered reflected their current needs. The registered manager had introduced a structured reassessment schedule, and supervising staff had completed updated assessments for the majority of people using the service. These assessments were more detailed and captured people’s preferences, routines, communication needs and levels of independence.
Care plans had been rewritten in line with these assessments. They now provided clearer step-by-step guidance for staff, including information about mobility support, nutritional requirements, preferred methods of communication and any risks identified.
Staff told us the revised care plans were easier to follow and gave them greater confidence in meeting people’s needs safely and consistently.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.
Staff demonstrated an improved understanding of consent and the principles of the Mental Capacity Act (2005) since the last inspection. Staff we spoke with described how they sought people’s consent before providing care, and we observed examples of staff offering choices and explaining tasks clearly.
Where people were able to make their own decisions, this was documented appropriately. For individuals whose capacity had changed, capacity assessments had been completed or reviewed, and best interest discussions were recorded where necessary. This ensured decisions reflected people’s wishes and legal requirements.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.
Staff had received updated training that was relevant to their roles and aligned with current best practice. This included refresher training in areas such as moving and handling, nutrition and hydration, and dementia awareness. New staff also completed an expanded induction programme that incorporated the Care Certificate standards.
The registered manager had begun cross-checking training content with recognised national guidelines to ensure it reflected evidence-based approaches. Care plans showed that staff were applying this learning in areas such as pressure area care, falls prevention and supporting people with long-term conditions.
People told us staff seemed more knowledgeable and better prepared during visits. One person said staff “explain what they’re doing now and check things properly,” which reflected the improved consistency of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager worked well across teams and services to support people. They made sure people only needed to tell their story once by sharing their assessment of needs when people moved between different services.
Staff worked effectively across teams and with external professionals to support people. Records showed that information from reassessments, risk reviews and GP or community nursing input was being shared appropriately with all relevant staff.
Where people moved between services—such as when returning home from a hospital stay—staff ensured essential information was relayed promptly so people did not need to repeat their story. We saw examples of staff consulting with hospital discharge teams, district nurses and occupational therapists to ensure equipment was in place and care arrangements had been updated before care restarted.
Staff told us communication between office and care teams had improved significantly, with a new daily handover process helping ensure consistency of support.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.
Staff routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to ensure outcomes were positive and continually improving. Daily visit logs, communication books and electronic monitoring records showed staff were noting people’s well being, any changes in their condition, and the support provided.
A person’s relative told us, “I think they are pretty good. They now do the checking in electronically and I can follow it on-line. I can see everything, including what they have done.”
The registered manager had introduced audits of care plans, visit notes and risk assessments to ensure outcomes aligned with people’s goals and clinical expectations. Where improvements were identified—such as updating mobility plans following therapy input or providing additional hydration prompts—these were acted upon and documented.
People and relatives told us they felt staff were more attentive and that care was becoming more consistent over time. Telling us, “They are always cheerful and happy and if late, they apologise. If (loved one) had a bad back and were in pain, they listen to them and adapt the approach in order to do it in a different manner.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager supported people to manage their health and well being to maximise their independence, choice and control. Staff supported people to live healthier lives and where possible, reduce their future needs for care and support.
Staff understood people’s day-to-day health needs and when concerns needed to be escalated. Records demonstrated staff had contacted people’s GP's, district nurses or family members promptly when changes were noted, including concerns about mobility, skin integrity, appetite, or mood. This helped ensure people received timely support and reduced the risk of deterioration.
People told us staff supported them well with hydration, nutrition and general well being. However, some feedback indicated that staff, particularly those new to the UK, were unfamiliar with certain local foods or how to prepare them to people’s preferences. This had occasionally resulted in meals being offered that people did not eat.
We fed this back to the nominated individual and registered manager. They told us this had already been identified, and plans were underway to introduce a practical workshop for overseas staff to learn about common local dishes, preparation techniques, and culturally appropriate drinks and snacks. This demonstrated a proactive approach to improving people’s experience of care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
Responsive – this means we looked for evidence that the provider met people’s needs.
At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people’s needs were met through good organisation and delivery.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager understood the diverse needs of the local community and ensured care was joined up and flexible.
The service primarily supported a community of Indian heritage, and cultural awareness had become a core part of the service’s approach.
The registered manager was supported by a supervisor who shared this cultural background. Together, they helped staff understand traditional practices, communication styles and expectations around food, family involvement, and daily routines. This helped ensure care was both culturally appropriate and inclusive. People told us they have consistency with who visited them and provided care and support. One person told us “We now get regular carers, so the stability is there now over the last year.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager made sure that people could access the care, support and treatment they needed when they needed it.

Staff ensured people could access the support they needed when required. The service aimed to be flexible, offering adjustments such as altering call times, adding extra visits, or cancelling calls at short notice when people requested this. People told us they appreciated this flexibility, especially when their health needs or family circumstances changed. One relative told us, “On occasions that someone can’t make it, then the replacement is always someone (my loved one) is familiar with.”

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
Staff and leaders actively listened to information about people who are most likely to experience inequality in experience or outcomes and tailored their care, support and treatment in response to this.
Staff and leaders listened closely to the experiences of those who may be at greater risk of unequal outcomes. For example, feedback from people with language barriers or specific cultural needs had led to improvements in communication, food preparation guidance and staff training.
A relative told us that they feel safe with the staff are supporting their loved one, “I feel good that they can communicate with the carers in (their native language).”
The service demonstrated a commitment to reducing inequality by adapting care practices and ensuring people’s voices were heard and acted upon.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager made it easy for people to share feedback and ideas, or raise complaints about their care, treatment and support. Staff involved people in decisions about their care and told them what had changed as a result.
The registered manager had made it easier for people to share their views. People were asked for feedback during regular reviews, informal check-in calls and through surveys. Complaints and concerns were logged, investigated and used to identify further improvements.
People told us they felt listened to and that office staff kept them informed about any changes to their care arrangements. Staff described involving people in daily decisions and adjusting support when people expressed new preferences or needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager made sure people were at the centre of their care and treatment choices and they decided, in partnership with people, how to respond to any relevant changes in people’s needs.
Staff ensured people were at the centre of decisions about their care and support. They worked in partnership with people and, where appropriate, their families to review care plans and respond to changes in their needs.
Since the last inspection, care plans had improved significantly. They were now highly personalised, detailed and written in a dignified and respectful way. Plans clearly described people’s preferences, routines, cultural considerations and health needs, supporting staff to provide care that aligned with what people wanted and valued.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
People were supported to plan for important life changes, so they could have enough time to make informed decisions about their future, including at the end of their life.
People were supported to plan for future life changes, including health decline and end-of-life care, at a pace that felt right for them. Where people did not wish to discuss these topics during their assessment, this was respected and clearly recorded, with plans to revisit the conversation when appropriate.
Staff had previously supported people receiving palliative care and had received relevant training. This meant the service was prepared to provide compassionate and sensitive support should end-of-life needs arise.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager supplied appropriate, accurate and up-to-date information in formats that were tailored to individual needs.
People received information in formats that suited their needs. The registered manager ensured policies, procedures and individual care records could be translated into people’s preferred languages on request. This supported people’s understanding of their care and their ability to make informed decisions.
Information about the service, such as how to raise concerns, what to expect from care and who to contact in an emergency, was provided clearly and accurately.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Safe – this means we looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm. At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant people were safe and protected from avoidable harm.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager assessed and managed the risk of infection. They detected and controlled the risk of it spreading and shared concerns with appropriate agencies promptly.
The registered manager had improved how infection risks were assessed and managed. Risks were identified, controlled and shared with appropriate agencies when necessary. Staff understood their responsibilities regarding the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) and told us PPE was accessible when needed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager worked with people to understand and manage risks by thinking holistically. Staff provided care to meet people’s needs that was safe, supportive and enabled people to do the things that mattered to them.
Processes for assessing risks had improved, but further work was required to ensure consistency. Risks to people’s health, safety and welfare were generally assessed, monitored and managed. Care plans and risk assessments were being reviewed and updated when needed. Plans were also in place to provide staff with additional mentoring to support their understanding of risk assessing.
During the inspection, we identified that risks relating to the use of flammable creams had not been fully assessed for some people. We raised this with the management team, who took immediate action. They confirmed these assessments would be rolled out to all relevant individuals, and the registered manager agreed to provide evidence once this had been completed.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager had a proactive and positive culture of safety, based on openness and honesty. Staff listened to concerns about safety and investigated and reported safety events. Lessons were learnt to continually identify and embed good practice.
At the last inspection, the service did not demonstrate a proactive or positive safety culture. Concerns were not consistently listened to, safety incidents were not always investigated or reported, and lessons were not learned to promote continuous improvement.
Since then, improvements had been made. The registered manager, who was not in post at the time of the previous inspection, told us they accepted the findings and implemented a clear plan to improve the service on taking up the role. There was now a more open culture within the management team, who were clear about the improvements required and demonstrated a commitment to strengthening safety practices across the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager did not always make sure that medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. Staff did not always involve people in planning.
At the last inspection, the provider had failed to ensure the safe management of medicines. While improvements had been made, these required further embedding into day-to-day practice. We found occasions where there were gaps in people’s medicines administration records. We queried this with the management team, who explained the reasons and agreed to add additional checks to medicines audits to ensure they could assure themselves that medicines were administered as prescribed.
Staff responsible for administering medicines had received training and competency assessments.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager made sure there were enough qualified, skilled and experienced staff, who received effective support, supervision and development. They worked together well to provide safe care that met people’s individual needs.
At the last inspection, the provider had not ensured there were enough suitably skilled and experienced staff, nor had staff received effective support or supervision. Improvements had since been made.
The registered manager had implemented strengthened recruitment checks to ensure new and existing staff were safe and suitable to work in people’s homes.There had been significant staff changes since the previous inspection, which people and staff told us had been positive.
Training and induction processes had been redeveloped, with evidence of mandatory training and shadowing shifts being completed. Staff said the training they received equipped them well to meet people’s needs. Staff were also receiving regular supervision, and a clear schedule of spot checks, supervisions and appraisals was now in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment. They made sure equipment, facilities and technology supported the delivery of safe care.
The registered manager had improved how environmental risks were identified and controlled. Since the last inspection, trained staff had begun assessing the safety of the home environments where care was provided and documenting these in environmental risk assessments. This helped ensure care was delivered safely for people and for staff supporting them.
Staff told us they ensured people’s homes were left tidy and secure after visits, including locking doors and key safes and ensuring people wore their personal alarms where required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager worked with people and healthcare partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care, in which safety was managed or monitored. They made sure there was continuity of care, including when people moved between different services.
Systems to support people’s safety had been strengthened. Assessments were carried out prior to care commencing, and information was shared with staff to support safe delivery of care. In response to the concerns found at the last inspection, the registered manager had overhauled several key processes, including those relating to hospital discharges and communication between teams, to ensure safe and well-managed transitions were in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager worked with people and healthcare partners to understand what being safe meant to them and the best way to achieve that. Staff concentrated on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live in safety, free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The registered manager shared concerns quickly and appropriately.
There had been improvements in safeguarding practices since the last inspection. The registered manager worked collaboratively with people and partner agencies to understand what feeling safe meant to each individual and how best to support this. Staff focused on improving people’s lives while protecting their right to live free from bullying, harassment, abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect. The management team shared concerns promptly and appropriately.
People told us they felt safe with staff and were confident any concerns they raised would be addressed. Staff had received safeguarding training, understood the signs of possible abuse and knew the steps to take should they have concerns. Staff also had access to the service’s updated safeguarding and whistle blowing policies.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: Well-led – this means we looked for evidence that service leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture. At our last assessment we rated this key question Inadequate. At this assessment the rating has changed to good. This meant the service was consistently managed and well-led. Leaders and the culture they created promoted high-quality, person-centred care.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The provider now had inclusive leaders at all levels who understood the context in which they delivered care, treatment and support and embodied the culture and values of their workforce and organisation. Leaders had the skills, knowledge, experience and credibility to lead effectively. They did so with integrity, openness and honesty.
The registered manager and nominated individual were seen as approachable, supportive and committed to improving the service. Staff described leaders as fair, compassionate and willing to listen, and told us communication had improved since the previous inspection.
One person told us, “The management has improved a lot. I now do not worry. I have seen positive change since the new manager came in. The carers have also changed, and they are more caring and have a better understanding of the job.”
Leaders had the skills and knowledge needed to oversee the service; however, many of their improvements were still relatively new and had not yet had time to become fully embedded. The progress made since the last inspection was wholly positive.
Leaders understood the cultural needs of the community, particularly through the support of the supervisor who shared the heritage of many people using the service. This helped shape more inclusive and personalised approaches. However, leaders acknowledged more work was required to develop staff confidence in supporting people from unfamiliar cultural backgrounds.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager fostered a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.
Staff told us they felt more comfortable raising concerns since the new management team had been in post. They said managers were approachable, responded to issues quickly, and encouraged staff to speak openly during supervision or informal discussions. Whistleblowing and safeguarding policies had been updated, and staff demonstrated awareness of how to escalate concerns.
However, some staff told us that historically they did not feel listened to, and although this had improved, a few remained cautious about raising issues. Leaders acknowledged the need to rebuild trust and had begun implementing strategies to strengthen staff confidence, such as anonymous feedback channels and team-building sessions.
Overall, staff now felt safer to speak up, but the culture of openness was still developing and needed further embedding across the entire workforce.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager had clear responsibilities, roles, systems of accountability and good governance. They used these to manage and deliver good quality, sustainable care, treatment and support. They acted on the best information about risk, performance and outcomes, and shared this securely with others when appropriate.
Governance systems had improved since the last inspection but were not yet fully embedded or consistently effective. The registered manager had introduced a range of quality monitoring processes—including audits of care plans, medicines, call monitoring and risk assessments—but these were still developing and had not yet demonstrated sustained reliability.
For example, audits had identified issues such as incomplete MAR charts and gaps in risk assessments, yet these findings had not always resulted in timely, documented follow-up action. Whilst immediate improvements were made when concerns were raised during our inspection, the need for external prompting indicated that governance systems were not yet robust enough to identify and address issues independently.
Roles and responsibilities were clearer than before, and staff understood who to escalate concerns to. However, some staff told us they were still adjusting to new processes and that changes had been frequent, which made consistency difficult to achieve.
Although the service had made significant progress, the governance arrangements required further time and oversight to ensure they became embedded, sustainable and capable of driving continuous improvement without direct intervention from the management team.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager focused on continuous learning, innovation and improvement across the organisation and local system. They encouraged creative ways of delivering equality of experience, outcome and quality of life for people. They actively contributed to safe, effective practice and research.
The registered manager had begun establishing a culture of learning and improvement. New audits, enhanced training programmes, and reflective supervision were increasing staff skills and knowledge. Leaders sought and acted on feedback from people, families and staff to refine practices.
There were early signs of innovation, such as the proposed cultural food preparation workshops and the redesign of care plans to be more personalised and user-friendly.
However, improvements were still in their early stages and had not yet demonstrated sustained long-term impact. Some learning processes—such as analysing trends in incidents, complaints and care notes—were not yet fully developed.
The registered manager and nominated individual were clearly moving the service in the right direction but remained at an early phase of development in its improvement cycle.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 2 - Evidence shows some shortfalls in the standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager understood their duty to collaborate and work in partnership, so services worked seamlessly for people. They shared information and learning with partners and collaborated for improvement.
Staff consulted effectively with GPs, district nurses, hospital discharge teams and community support networks. Feedback from professionals was generally positive, noting improved communication and responsiveness.
Work with the local community, particularly the Indian heritage community, had strengthened since our last inspection. Leaders used community insight to support culturally appropriate care planning and training.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager and the nominated individual had a shared vision, strategy and culture. This was based on transparency, equity, equality and human rights, diversity and inclusion, engagement, and understanding challenges and the needs of people and their communities.
The service demonstrated a clearer shared direction than at the last inspection. Staff understood the expectations of the new management team and told us the culture had improved, with more openness, communication and consistent expectations. The registered manager had introduced regular meetings, reflective supervision sessions and unannounced spot checks, which helped embed a more accountable culture.
People told us, “Yes, absolutely. I have seen a massive improvement in the last 6 months” and “Definitely have improved over the last year.”
The management team were visible, approachable and promoted a learning culture, but the service remained in a period of transition. Continued focus was required to ensure that the improvements introduced by the registered manager were sustained and consistently implemented by the whole team.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The registered manager valued diversity in their workforce. They worked towards an inclusive and fair culture by improving equality and equity for people who worked for them.
Staff from a range of cultural backgrounds were employed, and leaders had begun introducing training to improve cultural awareness and understanding—particularly important given the specific needs of the local community.
The registered manager and nominated individual were working to create a fair and inclusive culture, and staff told us they felt respected. However, there remained gaps in staff confidence, particularly around cultural sensitivity and communication, indicating that equality and inclusion initiatives were still in the initial stages of being fully embedded.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
